If the right branch already exists, `git switch right-branch` then `git cherry-pick <sha>`.
Switch back to the wrong branch: `git switch wrong-branch`.
Remove the commit from it with `git reset --hard HEAD~1` (only if not yet pushed).
Verify with `git log` on both branches that the commit landed where you wanted.
tips: If you hadn't pushed the wrong branch, `git switch -c right-branch` carries the commit over and you only need to reset the old one.
If the wrong branch was already pushed and shared, revert instead of reset.

guides.title: Fixing a rejected (non-fast-forward) push
steps: Read the error: 'rejected ... fetch first' means the remote has commits you don't have.
Run `git fetch origin` to download the remote's new commits without merging.
Inspect the divergence with `git log --oneline --graph HEAD origin/<branch>`.
Integrate them: `git rebase origin/<branch>` for a clean line, or `git merge origin/<branch>` to keep both.
Resolve any conflicts that surface, then continue (`git rebase --continue`).
Push again with `git push`; the fast-forward now succeeds.
tips: Never `git push --force` to fix this on a shared branch — you'll clobber teammates' commits.
Prefer `git push --force-with-lease` if you truly must force; it refuses if the remote moved unexpectedly.

guides.title: Aborting a merge in progress
steps: Confirm you're mid-merge: `git status` shows 'You have unmerged paths' or 'All conflicts fixed but you are still merging'.
If you haven't committed the merge yet, run `git merge --abort` to restore the pre-merge state.
If `merge --abort` complains, fall back to `git reset --hard HEAD` (loses uncommitted work).
Run `git status` to confirm you're back to a clean tree on your branch.
Re-check `git log --oneline -3` to ensure no merge commit was created.
tips: `merge --abort` only works while the merge is unfinished — once you commit, undo with `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD`.
`ORIG_HEAD` points to where you were before the merge started, a handy recovery anchor.

guides.title: Reverting a merge commit that was already pushed
steps: Find the merge commit's SHA with `git log --oneline --merges -5`.
Identify which parent to keep — usually `-m 1` keeps mainline, the branch you merged into.
Run `git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>` to create a new commit that undoes the merge.
Resolve any conflicts the revert raises, then complete it.
Push the revert commit normally with `git push`.
If you later want to re-merge that branch, you'll need to revert the revert first (Git considers it already merged).
tips: Use revert (not reset) for pushed merges — it's safe history that won't break collaborators.
Re-merging after a reverted merge is a known gotcha; note the revert SHA so you can revert it later.

guides.title: Stashing work to switch branches safely
steps: Run `git stash push -m "wip: feature x"` to shelve tracked changes with a label.
Add `-u` (`git stash push -u`) if you also need to stash untracked files.
Switch branches or pull as needed — your tree is now clean.
List your stashes any time with `git stash list`.
Reapply with `git stash pop` (applies and removes) or `git stash apply` (applies, keeps).
Resolve any conflicts the pop creates, then continue working.
tips: `pop` drops the stash even if applying caused conflicts — use `apply` if you want a safety copy.
Recover an accidentally dropped stash via `git fsck --no-reflogs | grep commit` then `git stash apply <sha>`.

guides.title: Recovering a dropped or lost stash
steps: First check `git stash list` in case it's still there under a different index.
If truly gone, run `git fsck --no-reflogs --unreachable | grep commit` to list dangling commits.
For each candidate SHA, inspect it with `git show <sha>` to find your stashed content.
Once found, restore it with `git stash apply <sha>`.
Verify your files are back, then commit or re-stash them properly.
If you remember a stash message, narrow the search with `git log --oneline --all --grep "wip"`.
tips: Stash commits are unreachable objects — they get garbage-collected, so recover quickly.
Stash objects show up as a commit with two or three parents in `git show`.

guides.title: Fixing a commit message
steps: For the most recent commit, run `git commit --amend` and edit the message in the editor.
If you also need to include new staged changes, stage them first, then `git commit --amend`.
To keep the same message and just add files, use `git commit --amend --no-edit`.
For an older commit, run `git rebase -i HEAD~N` covering that commit.
Change `pick` to `reword` next to the target commit, save, and edit its message when prompted.
If the commit was already pushed, you'll need `git push --force-with-lease` afterward.
tips: Amending rewrites the commit SHA — only safe before pushing or on personal branches.
Use `--force-with-lease` over `--force` to avoid overwriting someone else's pushes.

guides.title: Squashing several commits into one
steps: Count how many recent commits to combine, then run `git rebase -i HEAD~N`.
In the editor, leave the first commit as `pick`.
Change every following commit's `pick` to `squash` (or `fixup` to discard its message).
Save and close; Git opens a combined commit-message editor for the squashed commits.
Edit the final message, save, and let the rebase complete.
Push with `git push --force-with-lease` if these commits were already on the remote.
tips: `fixup` is like `squash` but silently drops that commit's message — great for 'oops typo' commits.
If a rebase conflict appears, fix it, `git add`, then `git rebase --continue`.
`git rebase --abort` bails out cleanly if it gets messy.

guides.title: Working through a rebase conflict
steps: When the rebase pauses, read the message naming the conflicting commit and files.
Run `git status` to see the unmerged paths.
Edit each file, removing the `<<<<<<<`/`=======`/`>>>>>>>` markers to the desired result.
Stage the resolutions with `git add <file>` for each.
Continue with `git rebase --continue`; repeat for any further conflicts.
If a commit's changes are now redundant, use `git rebase --skip`.
If overwhelmed, `git rebase --abort` returns you to the pre-rebase state.
tips: During a rebase, 'ours' and 'theirs' are swapped vs a merge — 'ours' is the branch you're rebasing onto.
Enable `git config rerere.enabled true` so Git remembers conflict resolutions if you redo the rebase.

guides.title: Removing a file from a commit
steps: If the commit is the latest, unstage the file: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, then `git restore --staged <file>`.
Recommit the remaining staged changes with `git commit -c ORIG_HEAD` to reuse the old message.
If you want the file gone from the working tree too, delete it before recommitting.
For an older commit, run `git rebase -i HEAD~N` and `edit` that commit.
When the rebase stops, `git rm --cached <file>` then `git commit --amend`.
Finish with `git rebase --continue` and force-push if it was already shared.
tips: `git rm --cached` removes the file from Git tracking but leaves it on disk.
Add the file to `.gitignore` so it doesn't get re-committed accidentally.

guides.title: Purging a leaked secret from history
steps: Immediately rotate/revoke the leaked credential — assume it is already compromised.
Install git-filter-repo (`pip install git-filter-repo`), the recommended modern tool.
From a fresh clone, run `git filter-repo --path secrets.env --invert-paths` to delete the file across all history.
Alternatively replace a string everywhere with `git filter-repo --replace-text replacements.txt`.
Force-push the rewritten history: `git push --force --all` and `git push --force --tags`.
Tell every collaborator to re-clone, since their old clones still contain the secret.
Add the file/pattern to `.gitignore` to prevent recurrence.
tips: Rotating the secret matters more than scrubbing — caches, forks, and CI logs may retain it.
git-filter-repo replaces the deprecated `filter-branch` and the BFG for most cases.

triggers: cannot pull local changes would be overwritten
your local changes would be overwritten
guides.title: Pulling when local changes block the merge
steps: Read the error: Git refuses to overwrite uncommitted edits to certain files.
Decide whether your local edits matter. If yes, stash them: `git stash push -m "before pull"`.
Run `git pull` now that the tree is clean.
Reapply your work with `git stash pop` and resolve any conflicts.
If your local edits were junk, discard them with `git restore <file>` then pull.
Verify with `git status` and `git log --oneline -3` that you're up to date.
tips: Stash-pull-pop is the safest dance when a pull is blocked by local changes.
Configure `git config pull.rebase true` to get a linear history on every pull.

guides.title: Restoring a deleted file from history
steps: If you only deleted it (not committed), run `git restore <file>` to bring it back.
If the deletion was committed, find the last commit that had it: `git log --oneline -- <file>`.
Note the SHA just before the deletion commit.
Restore the file from that commit: `git checkout <sha>~1 -- <file>` (or `git restore --source=<sha> <file>`).
Stage and commit the restored file with `git add <file> && git commit`.
If you don't know the path, search history with `git log --all --diff-filter=D --name-only`.
tips: `--diff-filter=D` filters the log to deletion events, handy when you forgot the filename.
`git checkout <sha> -- <file>` (no `~1`) grabs the version AT that commit instead of before it.

guides.title: Removing a large file bloating the repo
steps: Find the biggest objects: `git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check | sort -k3 -n | tail`.
Confirm the offending blob's path from the output.
Use git-filter-repo to strip it: `git filter-repo --path bigfile.zip --invert-paths`.
If the file is still needed going forward, track it via Git LFS instead and re-add it.
Run `git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now --aggressive` to reclaim space.
Force-push the rewritten history and have collaborators re-clone.
tips: GitHub rejects pushes over 100 MB per file — Git LFS is the supported workaround.
Add large binary patterns to `.gitignore` and `.gitattributes` (for LFS) to prevent re-bloat.

guides.title: Fixing a wrong remote URL
steps: List current remotes and their URLs with `git remote -v`.
Update the URL with `git remote set-url origin <new-url>`.
Re-run `git remote -v` to confirm the change took.
Test connectivity with `git fetch origin`.
If you need to add a second remote, use `git remote add upstream <url>` instead of overwriting origin.
Push to confirm the pipeline works: `git push -u origin <branch>`.
tips: Switching SSH↔HTTPS auth is the usual reason to set-url — match it to your credential setup.
`git remote rename old new` and `git remote remove name` round out remote management.

guides.title: Fixing Git authentication failures
steps: Read the error: 'Permission denied (publickey)' is SSH; '401'/'invalid username or password' is HTTPS.
For SSH, test with `ssh -T git@github.com` to see if your key is accepted.
If not, ensure your key is loaded: `ssh-add -l`, then `ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`.
Confirm the public key is registered in your Git host's account settings.
For HTTPS, GitHub no longer accepts passwords — generate a personal access token and use it as the password.
Update stored credentials: clear the keychain entry or run `git credential reject`, then retry the push.
tips: Check the remote scheme with `git remote -v` — SSH (`git@`) vs HTTPS need totally different auth.
Use a credential helper (`git config --global credential.helper`) so you only enter the token once.

guides.title: Unstaging files you added by mistake
steps: Run `git status` to see what's currently staged (under 'Changes to be committed').
Unstage a single file with `git restore --staged <file>` (or `git reset HEAD <file>` on old Git).
Unstage everything at once with `git restore --staged .`.
Confirm the file moved back to 'Changes not staged for commit' via `git status`.
Your edits are preserved — unstaging never touches working-tree content.
Re-stage only what you want with `git add -p` for fine-grained control.
tips: Unstaging is safe: it only affects the index, not your actual file contents.
`git add -p` lets you stage individual hunks so you don't over-commit next time.

guides.title: Finding the commit that introduced a bug with bisect
steps: Start the session with `git bisect start`.
Mark the current broken state: `git bisect bad`.
Mark a known-good older commit: `git bisect good <sha-or-tag>`.
Git checks out a midpoint commit — test it, then run `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`.
Repeat until Git prints '<sha> is the first bad commit'.
End the session with `git bisect reset` to return to your original branch.
Inspect the culprit with `git show <sha>`.
tips: Automate it: `git bisect run ./test.sh` lets a script return non-zero for 'bad' and bisect everything for you.
Bisect does a binary search, so even hundreds of commits resolve in a handful of tests.

guides.title: Fixing a .gitignore that isn't working
steps: Understand the cause: .gitignore only affects UNtracked files; already-tracked files keep being tracked.
Confirm with `git check-ignore -v <file>` which rule (if any) matches.
If the file is already tracked, stop tracking it: `git rm --cached <file>` (keeps it on disk).
For a whole tracked directory, use `git rm -r --cached <dir>`.
Verify the .gitignore pattern is correct (no leading slash issues, no trailing spaces).
Commit the removal; the file now stays ignored going forward.
tips: `git check-ignore -v` tells you the exact file:line of the rule deciding the file's fate.
A trailing space or wrong path anchor (`/build` vs `build/`) is the usual silent culprit.

triggers: restore single file from another branch
guides.title: Pulling a single file from another branch
steps: Make sure your working tree is clean or your edits to that file are saved.
Run `git restore --source=<branch> -- path/to/file` (modern syntax).
On older Git, use `git checkout <branch> -- path/to/file`.
The file now reflects the other branch's version but stays staged on your current branch.
Review the change with `git diff --staged path/to/file`.
Commit it as usual if you want to keep that version.
tips: This grabs only one file — your current branch is otherwise untouched.
Use `git show <branch>:path/to/file` to peek at the other branch's version without changing anything.

guides.title: Clearing a stuck index.lock
steps: Read the error: 'Unable to create .git/index.lock: File exists.'
First make sure no other Git process is actually running (check editors, IDEs, background tasks).
Verify with `ps aux | grep git` that nothing legitimate holds the lock.
If nothing is running, the lock is stale — delete it: `rm -f .git/index.lock`.
Retry your original Git command.
If other `.lock` files appear (e.g. `HEAD.lock`, `<ref>.lock`), remove those too once you've confirmed no process owns them.
tips: Deleting index.lock while a real Git process runs can corrupt the index — always confirm it's stale first.
IDEs that auto-run Git (VS Code, JetBrains) are the most common cause of phantom locks.

guides.title: Fixing the wrong author on a commit
steps: Set your correct identity first: `git config user.name "Name"` and `git config user.email you@example.com`.
For the latest commit, run `git commit --amend --reset-author --no-edit`.
Confirm with `git log -1 --format='%an <%ae>'`.
For older commits, run `git rebase -i HEAD~N` and `edit` the target, then `git commit --amend --reset-author`.
To rewrite author across all history, use `git filter-repo --mailmap mailmap.txt`.
Force-push with `--force-with-lease` if the commits were already pushed.
tips: Set `--global` config so future repos don't repeat the mistake.
A `.mailmap` file can also just remap names in logs without rewriting history if that's enough.

guides.title: Recovering a deleted branch
steps: Run `git reflog` and look for the last commit that was on the deleted branch.
Alternatively, if you remember the tip SHA, skip straight to recreating it.
Recreate the branch at that commit: `git branch <name> <sha>`.
Switch to it with `git switch <name>` and verify `git log --oneline -5`.
If the branch only existed on the remote, fetch it back: `git fetch origin <name>:<name>`.
Push it back up if needed with `git push -u origin <name>`.
tips: Deleting a branch only removes the pointer — the commits survive in reflog until garbage collection.
`git branch -D` (force delete) still leaves the commits recoverable via reflog for ~30 days.

triggers: apply one commit to another branch
guides.title: Cherry-picking a commit onto another branch
steps: Find the commit SHA you want with `git log --oneline` on its source branch.
Switch to the destination branch: `git switch target-branch`.
Apply it with `git cherry-pick <sha>` (use a range `A..B` for several).
If a conflict appears, resolve the files, `git add` them, then `git cherry-pick --continue`.
To bail out, run `git cherry-pick --abort`.
Verify with `git log --oneline -3` that the commit landed on the right branch.
tips: Cherry-pick creates a NEW commit with a different SHA — the original stays put.
Use `-x` (`git cherry-pick -x <sha>`) to append the source SHA to the message for traceability.

triggers: git status shows all files changed
guides.title: Fixing line-ending churn that marks everything changed
steps: Confirm the cause with `git diff` — if changes are whole-file with no visible edits, it's line endings.
Check your setting: `git config core.autocrlf` (Windows often needs `true`, mac/Linux `input`).
Add a `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto` to normalize endings repo-wide.
Renormalize the index: `git add --renormalize .`.
Commit the normalization in one dedicated commit so the noise is isolated.
Confirm `git status` is clean afterward and others pull the `.gitattributes`.
tips: `.gitattributes` is the durable fix; per-machine `core.autocrlf` settings drift between teammates.
Pin specific binary or shell-script endings (`*.sh text eol=lf`) to avoid breaking executables.

triggers: ci passes locally but fails on ci
tests pass locally fail in ci
guides.title: CI fails but everything passes locally
steps: Compare the exact command CI runs versus what you run locally — read the workflow/pipeline YAML, not your memory of it.
Check the runner's OS, language version, and locale against your machine; mismatched Node/Python/Java versions are the usual culprit.
Look for files CI cannot see: anything in .gitignore, uncommitted changes, or local-only env vars and dotfiles.
Reproduce the environment in a clean container (e.g. docker run the same base image) and run the failing command there.
Disable any test caching and run with a fresh checkout to rule out stale artifacts.
Add the failing step's full logs with verbose flags and re-run to capture the divergence point.
tips: Filesystem case-sensitivity bites here: macOS is case-insensitive, most Linux CI runners are not.
Pin tool versions in CI so an upstream minor bump doesn't silently change behavior.

guides.title: Resolve a Git merge conflict
steps: Run `git status` to list the files marked as 'both modified'.
Open each conflicted file and find the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` markers.
Decide the correct final content for each block — keep yours, keep theirs, or combine — and delete all three marker lines.
Stage each resolved file with `git add <file>`.
Run `git status` again to confirm no files remain unmerged.
Finish with `git commit` (for a merge) or `git rebase --continue` (for a rebase).
tips: `git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort` safely backs out if you want to start over.
Use `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U` to list only the still-conflicted files.

guides.title: npm install / npm ci fails in the build
steps: Read the first error in the log, not the last — the root cause is usually near the top (a peer-dep or registry error).
Confirm a `package-lock.json` exists and is committed; `npm ci` hard-fails without a lockfile in sync with package.json.
Delete `node_modules` and the lockfile locally, run `npm install`, and commit the regenerated lockfile if it changed.
Check the Node version: run `node -v` and compare to the `engines` field and the CI runner version.
If a private registry or token is involved, verify `.npmrc` and the auth token are present in the CI environment.
Re-run with `npm install --verbose` (or `npm ci --foreground-scripts`) to see which package's postinstall script is breaking.
tips: `npm ci` requires package.json and package-lock.json to match exactly — regenerate the lock if you hand-edited deps.
Network flakiness shows as ETIMEDOUT/ECONNRESET; add a registry mirror or retry before assuming a real failure.

guides.title: Debug a failing Docker build
steps: Note the exact step number in the build output where it fails — Docker prints `Step N/M` (or the `[stage x/y]` line with BuildKit).
Re-run the build with `--progress=plain --no-cache` so you see full output and rule out a poisoned cache layer.
If a `RUN` command fails, reproduce it interactively: `docker run -it <last-good-image-id> sh` and run the command by hand.
Check that every `COPY`/`ADD` source path exists and isn't excluded by `.dockerignore`.
Verify the base image tag still exists and pin it to a digest if it was a moving tag like `:latest`.
For network failures inside RUN, confirm the build has DNS/proxy access (corporate proxies need ARG/ENV http_proxy).
tips: Order Dockerfile layers from least- to most-frequently-changed so the cache survives small edits.
BuildKit hides successful step output by default — `--progress=plain` brings it back.

triggers: remote contains work you do not have
guides.title: git push rejected (non-fast-forward)
steps: Read the message: a rejection means the remote branch has commits your local branch doesn't.
Run `git fetch origin` to pull down the remote's latest refs without merging.
Integrate the remote work: `git rebase origin/<branch>` (linear) or `git merge origin/<branch>` (merge commit).
Resolve any conflicts that surface, then continue the rebase/merge.
Run your tests locally to confirm the integration didn't break anything.
Push again with `git push`; only use `--force-with-lease` if you intentionally rewrote history and own the branch.
tips: Never `git push --force` to a shared branch — `--force-with-lease` refuses if someone else pushed in the meantime.
If you see this on a protected branch, you likely need to open a PR instead of pushing directly.

guides.title: Environment variable or secret missing in CI/CD
steps: Identify which variable is undefined from the error, then echo a masked check in CI (e.g. `echo "set: ${VAR:+yes}"`) — never echo the raw secret.
Confirm the secret is defined in the right scope: repo vs org vs environment, and that the job actually has access to that environment.
Check that the variable name in the workflow matches exactly, including case, and that it's mapped into the step's `env:` block.
For pull requests from forks, remember secrets are usually withheld for security — verify the trigger type.
Ensure the secret isn't being consumed in a context that runs before it's injected (e.g. a reusable workflow that wasn't passed the secret).
Re-run the job after fixing the mapping; secrets are read at job start, not retroactively.
tips: CI masks known secret values in logs, but env vars derived from them may leak — avoid printing them at all.
Fork PRs intentionally lack secrets; use a separate workflow with manual approval for those.

guides.title: Build fails with 'no space left on device'
steps: Confirm the failure: 'ENOSPC' or 'no space left on device' in the log points at disk, not memory.
Add a `df -h` step before the failing command to see which mount is full.
Clean build caches and Docker cruft early: `docker system prune -af`, remove `node_modules`/build dirs you no longer need.
Check for runaway artifacts — large logs, core dumps, or duplicate downloaded dependencies filling the workspace.
If on a hosted runner, free preinstalled bloat (e.g. remove unused SDKs) or switch to a larger runner size.
Trim what you cache: cache only the dependency directory, not the entire build output.
tips: inode exhaustion looks like ENOSPC even with free bytes — check `df -i` too.
Multi-stage Docker builds and a tight `.dockerignore` keep image and context size down.

guides.title: Diagnose a flaky test in CI
steps: Confirm flakiness: re-run the same commit several times and see if the result varies without code changes.
Run the suspect test in isolation and then repeatedly (loop it 50-100x) to make the failure reproduce on demand.
Look for shared mutable state: global singletons, the database, the filesystem, or test order dependence.
Check timing assumptions — hard-coded sleeps, real timestamps, timezones, or races on async work.
Pin or seed anything random (RNG seed, faker seed, fixed clock) and re-run.
Once reproduced, fix the root cause (isolate state / await properly) rather than adding a retry.
tips: Run tests in random order locally to surface order-dependence the CI runner may already use.
A blanket retry hides flakiness but lets the real bug ship — quarantine, then fix.

guides.title: Recover from a detached HEAD state
steps: Run `git status` — 'HEAD detached at <hash>' confirms you're not on a branch.
If you made commits here you want to keep, note the current commit hash from `git log -1`.
Create a branch to capture the work: `git branch save-work` (or `git switch -c save-work`).
If you made no commits and just want out, `git switch <your-branch>` (or `git checkout main`).
Verify with `git status` that you're now on a named branch.
If you already switched away and think you lost commits, find them with `git reflog` and `git branch recover <hash>`.
tips: Detached HEAD is normal after `git checkout <tag>` or `<hash>` — it only becomes a problem if you commit and walk away.
`git reflog` remembers where HEAD has been for ~90 days; almost nothing is truly lost.

guides.title: pip install fails in the build
steps: Read the first failing package in the log; resolver errors and wheel-build errors have very different fixes.
Confirm the Python version matches what the package supports — many wheels are version- and platform-specific.
If you see 'could not build wheel', install the system build deps (compiler, headers like python3-dev, libpq-dev) for that package.
For 'no matching distribution', check the package name spelling, the index URL, and any required extra-index for private packages.
Pin versions with a lockfile (pip-tools, Poetry, or `pip freeze`) so the resolver isn't choosing new majors on every run.
Re-run with `pip install -v` to see whether it's a download, resolve, or compile failure.
tips: Always build inside a fresh virtualenv in CI so system packages don't mask missing deps.
A failing wheel build on Alpine is usually musl vs glibc — use a slim Debian base or install build-base.

triggers: deploy succeeded but site is old
guides.title: Deploy succeeds but users still see the old version
steps: Confirm the deploy actually shipped the new build artifact — check the artifact hash/commit SHA in the deploy logs.
Hard-refresh the browser (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+R) and check in a private window to rule out local browser cache.
Inspect response headers for `Cache-Control`/`ETag`; long max-age on HTML means the CDN/browser keeps serving old.
Purge or invalidate the CDN cache for the changed paths after deploy.
Verify you're hitting the right environment/host — DNS or a load balancer may still point at the old release.
Add a cache-busting query string or content hash to filenames so updated assets get unique URLs.
tips: Never cache HTML aggressively; cache only fingerprinted assets (e.g. app.abc123.js) with long max-age.
Blue/green or rolling deploys can leave you talking to the old instance — check which target served the request.

guides.title: CI workflow YAML won't parse
steps: Run the file through a YAML linter (`yamllint`) or the provider's config validator to get the exact line/column.
Check indentation: YAML requires spaces, never tabs, and consistent depth for nested keys.
Quote values that contain special characters (`:`, `#`, leading `*`/`!`, version strings like `3.10` that parse as floats).
Verify list vs map: a leading `-` makes a list item, while `key:` makes a mapping — mixing them breaks parsing.
Watch for duplicate keys at the same level; many parsers silently take the last one or error out.
Re-validate after each fix; YAML errors often cascade, so the reported line may be after the real mistake.
tips: `on:` and version numbers are classic gotchas — `on` can be read as boolean true, `3.10` as the float 3.1.
Editor's YAML extension with schema validation catches most of these before you push.

guides.title: Debug a failing Gradle build
steps: Re-run with `./gradlew build --stacktrace --info` to see the failing task and full cause.
Add `--scan` (or read the failure summary) to identify whether it's compilation, a test, or dependency resolution.
For dependency errors, run `./gradlew dependencies` to inspect the resolved graph and spot version conflicts.
Confirm the JDK version matches the project's `sourceCompatibility`/toolchain; a wrong JDK fails compilation cryptically.
Clear stale state with `./gradlew --stop` then `clean`, and if needed delete `~/.gradle/caches` for corrupt artifacts.
Use the committed `gradlew` wrapper, not a globally installed Gradle, so the version is reproducible.
tips: Run `--no-daemon` in CI to avoid a stale daemon carrying corrupt state between jobs.
Gradle's dependency cache can hold a corrupt download — `--refresh-dependencies` forces re-fetch.

guides.title: 'Permission denied' running a script in CI
steps: Read whether it's 'Permission denied' (executable bit) or 'bad interpreter' (shebang/line endings).
Make the script executable and commit the bit: `git update-index --chmod=+x script.sh` (or `chmod +x` then commit).
Check the shebang line is correct and on line 1 (`#!/usr/bin/env bash`), with no BOM before it.
Confirm line endings are LF, not CRLF — CRLF turns the interpreter path into an invalid name ('bad interpreter').
For 'exec format error', verify you're not running a binary built for a different architecture (arm64 vs amd64).
Re-run the job after committing the executable bit and line-ending fix.
tips: Add `* text=auto eol=lf` (and `*.sh text eol=lf`) in `.gitattributes` to stop Windows checkouts from CRLF-ing scripts.
`git ls-files -s script.sh` shows mode 100755 when the executable bit is committed.

guides.title: CI job times out or hangs
steps: Find where it hangs: look at the last log line before the timeout — that's the command that never returned.
Check for a process waiting on input (interactive prompts); add `--yes`/non-interactive flags or pipe `< /dev/null`.
Look for a server started in the foreground without `&` so the step never proceeds to the next command.
Verify network calls aren't silently retrying forever; add explicit connect/read timeouts.
Reduce the timeout temporarily to fail fast and capture logs, then reproduce locally with the same flags.
Once found, fix the root cause and set a sane per-step timeout so future hangs fail quickly.
tips: A background server should be started with `&` and then waited on with a readiness poll, not a fixed sleep.
Tools that detect a TTY behave differently in CI — force non-interactive mode explicitly.

guides.title: CI cache never hits (always cold)
steps: Inspect the cache step logs for 'cache not found' vs 'cache restored' to confirm it's truly missing.
Check the cache key: if it includes a value that changes every run (timestamp, run id, full SHA), it will never hit.
Build the key from a stable hash of the lockfile (e.g. hash of package-lock.json) so it changes only when deps change.
Confirm the cached path matches where the tool actually stores files (npm cache dir vs node_modules differ).
Verify the cache was saved on a prior successful run — the first run is always a miss by design.
Add a restore-keys fallback so a partial/older cache can still be reused when the exact key misses.
tips: Cache the package manager's cache dir, not the installed output, for the most reliable hits.
Branch scoping matters: many CI systems isolate caches per branch and only fall back to the default branch's cache.

guides.title: A secret was committed to Git
steps: Rotate the secret immediately — assume it's compromised the moment it hit a remote, even if you delete it.
Stop pushing; the priority is invalidating the leaked credential, not just hiding it.
Remove it from history with `git filter-repo --replace-text` (preferred) or BFG Repo-Cleaner, targeting the file/string.
Force-push the rewritten history and coordinate with collaborators to re-clone (rewriting shared history breaks their clones).
Add the file/pattern to `.gitignore` and move the value into a secrets manager or CI secret store.
Add a pre-commit secret scanner (gitleaks/trufflehog) so it can't happen again.
tips: Deleting in a new commit does NOT remove the secret — it stays in history and in forks/caches.
GitHub and others cache and even index pushed commits; rotation is non-negotiable.

guides.title: 'Cannot find module' in the build but not locally
steps: Read the exact module name in the error — note whether it's a package or a relative path.
If it's a package, confirm it's in `dependencies` (not `devDependencies`) when needed at build/runtime in production installs.
If it's a relative path, check the import's case exactly: Linux CI is case-sensitive, your laptop may not be.
Confirm the file extension and path are real, and that it isn't excluded by `.gitignore` (so CI never checked it out).
Verify the dependency is actually in the committed lockfile and that `npm ci` ran successfully before the build.
Reproduce with a clean install (`rm -rf node_modules && npm ci`) locally to mirror CI.
tips: `./Components/Button` vs `./components/Button` works on macOS/Windows but fails on Linux runners.
A package that only exists locally (linked or globally installed) won't be in the lockfile — add it explicitly.

guides.title: Roll back a bad production deploy
steps: Confirm the deploy is the cause: check the deploy timestamp against when errors/alerts started.
Trigger your platform's rollback to the previous known-good release (most PaaS keep prior releases one click away).
If there's no built-in rollback, redeploy the previous commit/tag explicitly rather than reverting code under pressure.
Verify health checks and key user flows on the rolled-back version before declaring recovery.
Hold any database migration concerns: if the bad deploy migrated the schema, rollback of code may not be enough — plan a forward-compatible fix.
After recovery, `git revert` the bad commit on main so the fix is captured in history, then investigate calmly.
tips: Backward-incompatible migrations make rollbacks dangerous — use expand/contract migrations so old and new code both work.
Keep the previous build artifact around; rebuilding from source during an incident wastes precious minutes.

guides.title: Git LFS errors in CI checkout
steps: Identify the failure: 'smudge filter lfs failed', 'object does not exist', or a quota/bandwidth message.
Confirm Git LFS is installed on the runner and that the checkout step has `lfs: true` enabled.
Check whether the LFS storage quota or bandwidth limit was hit on the host — that blocks downloads.
Verify the pointer files were actually pushed: a committed pointer with no uploaded object causes 'object does not exist'.
Run `git lfs fetch --all` / `git lfs pull` to retrieve objects, and `git lfs ls-files` to confirm tracking.
If you don't need binaries for a job, set `GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1` to skip the download entirely.
tips: Shallow clones plus LFS can miss objects — ensure the checkout fetches LFS for the needed commits.
Track the right patterns in `.gitattributes`; an untracked large file just bloats the repo instead of using LFS.

guides.title: Kubernetes ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull
steps: Run `kubectl describe pod <pod>` and read the Events at the bottom for the exact pull error.
Verify the image name and tag are correct and that the tag actually exists in the registry.
For 'unauthorized'/'denied', confirm an imagePullSecret is configured and referenced by the pod's service account.
Check the registry hostname is reachable from the cluster (private registry, VPC, or firewall rules).
Confirm the image architecture matches the node (arm64 image on amd64 nodes fails to run even after pulling).
Re-deploy after fixing creds/tag; the kubelet retries automatically with exponential backoff.
tips: `:latest` is a moving target — pin a specific tag or digest so deploys are reproducible.
Rate limits (e.g. Docker Hub anonymous pulls) show as pull failures; authenticate or mirror the image.

guides.title: A Git pre-commit hook keeps failing
steps: Read the hook's output — it names the check that failed (lint, format, type-check, tests).
Run that check manually outside the hook to get the full, unfiltered error and fix the underlying issue.
Confirm the hook tool is installed (e.g. `husky`/`pre-commit` set up) and its dependencies are present in node_modules/venv.
Check the hook isn't failing on staged vs working-tree mismatch — `lint-staged` only sees staged files, so stage your fixes.
Verify the hook script is executable and uses the right interpreter path.
If you must commit past a broken hook in an emergency, `git commit --no-verify` — then fix and re-run the check in CI.
tips: `--no-verify` skips hooks locally but CI will still run the same checks — don't rely on it to ship.
Hooks live in `.husky/` or `.git/hooks`; a fresh clone may not have them installed until you run the setup command.

guides.title: Build runs out of memory (OOM killed)
steps: Spot the signature: 'JavaScript heap out of memory', 'Killed', or exit code 137 all mean OOM.
Check the runner's memory limit and compare to the build's peak usage; default hosted runners are often small.
Raise the tool's heap ceiling where applicable (e.g. `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=4096`) up to the runner's RAM.
Reduce parallelism — limit concurrent test workers or compiler jobs (`--maxWorkers`, `-j N`) so each uses less RAM.
Split a giant build into smaller chunks or enable incremental/cached builds to lower peak memory.
If still tight, move the job to a larger runner with more RAM.
tips: Exit code 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL), the kernel's OOM killer — not your code throwing.
Setting heap above the container's actual memory just delays the kill; size both together.

guides.title: TLS/SSL certificate errors during build or deploy
steps: Read the exact error: 'certificate has expired', 'self signed certificate in chain', or 'unable to get local issuer'.
Check the date on the runner — a wrong system clock makes valid certs look expired.
If it's a corporate proxy injecting its own CA, add that CA to the trust store (update-ca-certificates) inside the build.
For an expired endpoint cert, that's a server fix — renew it; don't disable verification.
Confirm the full certificate chain is served by the endpoint (a missing intermediate causes 'unable to get local issuer').
Re-run after fixing trust; verify with `openssl s_client -connect host:443` showing the chain and 'Verify return code: 0'.
tips: Disabling TLS verification (`NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0`, `-k`) hides the bug and is unsafe — fix the trust chain instead.
A cert that works in browsers but fails in CLI tools usually means a missing intermediate cert.

guides.title: Git submodules empty or failing to clone in CI
steps: Confirm symptom: the submodule directory is empty or checkout errors with 'fatal: No url found for submodule path'.
Tell the checkout to include submodules (e.g. set `submodules: true`/`recursive` on the checkout step).
If running git manually, use `git submodule update --init --recursive` after clone.
Check authentication: private submodules over SSH need a deploy key or token the runner can use.
Verify `.gitmodules` URLs are reachable from CI — swap SSH URLs for HTTPS+token if SSH isn't configured.
Confirm the committed submodule pointer references a commit that still exists in the submodule repo.
tips: Shallow clones may skip submodules — explicitly enable recursive submodule fetch.
Mixing SSH submodule URLs with an HTTPS-token CI checkout fails; normalize the URL scheme via `insteadOf` or .gitmodules.

triggers: ci runs on every push unexpectedly
guides.title: Pipeline triggers on the wrong branch or not at all
steps: Read the workflow's trigger config (`on:` / pipeline rules) and list exactly which branches/events it matches.
Confirm the event that occurred (push vs pull_request vs tag) matches a configured trigger.
Check branch filters and path filters: a `paths:` filter can skip the run if no matching files changed.
Verify the file is on the default branch — many CI systems only read workflow definitions from there for certain events.
Look for a separate condition (`if:`) inside the job that silently skips it.
Re-trigger with the corrected filters and watch the run list to confirm it fires for the intended branch.
tips: pull_request events run the workflow from the base branch's config, not the PR branch's — edits to triggers won't apply until merged.
Path filters are easy to get wrong; a leading `/` or wrong glob can match nothing.

triggers: build output missing in next stage
guides.title: Artifacts not passing between CI jobs
steps: Confirm the upload step actually ran and reported success in the producing job's logs.
Check the path you uploaded matches where the build wrote the files — a wrong glob uploads nothing.
Verify the artifact name used to download exactly matches the name used to upload.
Ensure the downloading job depends on (waits for) the uploading job, or it may run first with nothing to fetch.
Confirm the artifact hasn't expired (retention windows) and that both jobs are in the same run/workflow.
Re-run and inspect the artifact listing to confirm size and contents before the consuming step.
tips: Uploading an empty directory often succeeds silently — assert the file exists before uploading.
Separate jobs don't share a workspace; you must explicitly upload/download to pass files between them.

triggers: typescript build error not in editor
type check passes locally fails ci
guides.title: TypeScript compiles in the editor but fails in CI
steps: Run the exact CI command locally — usually `tsc --noEmit` (or the build's type-check), not just relying on the editor.
Confirm the TypeScript version in CI matches your local one; a different `typescript` version changes diagnostics.
Check that the editor isn't using a looser config — CI uses tsconfig.json with `strict`, the editor may suppress some errors.
Look for skipped files: `skipLibCheck` or excluded paths may differ, surfacing errors only in the full build.
Verify `@types/*` packages are in the lockfile and installed in CI (missing types pass in editor with cached state).
Fix the reported errors, then re-run `tsc --noEmit` until clean before pushing.
tips: Editors cache stale type info; a clean `tsc --noEmit` is the source of truth.
A devDependency type package missing from the lockfile fails CI but not your warm local cache.

guides.title: Authentication fails during deploy or registry push
steps: Read whether it's 401 (bad/missing credentials) or 403 (authenticated but lacking permission) — they have different fixes.
For 401, verify the token/key is present in CI, not expired, and passed to the login/deploy step's environment.
For 403, check the service account/role has the specific permission (push to this registry, deploy to this project).
Confirm the login step ran before the push/deploy step and that its session is still valid in the same job.
Check for region/account mismatches — pushing to the wrong registry account returns denied.
Rotate the credential if it may be expired or revoked, update the secret, and re-run.
tips: Short-lived OIDC/federated tokens expire mid-job for long builds — refresh or shorten the build.
A credential that works locally may have broader scopes than the CI service account; match the permissions explicitly.

guides.title: Database migration fails during deploy
steps: Read the migration error — it names the failing statement (duplicate column, lock timeout, constraint violation).
Check the migration history table to see which migrations applied and where it stopped (partial state is the danger).
For a lock timeout, find the blocking query/long transaction holding the table and resolve it before retrying.
If it failed mid-way, determine whether the failed migration is transactional; if not, you may need a manual fix-up.
Test the migration against a copy of production data, not an empty dev DB, to catch data-dependent failures.
Adopt expand/contract (add nullable column, backfill, then enforce) so a migration never blocks or breaks running app code.
tips: Adding a NOT NULL column with no default, or an index without CONCURRENTLY, can lock a large table and time out.
Run migrations as a separate, idempotent deploy step so an app rollback doesn't leave schema and code mismatched.

triggers: fatal javascript heap out of memory
guides.title: Track down a Node.js memory leak
steps: Reproduce the growth: run the workload for a few minutes and watch RSS with `node --max-old-space-size=512 app.js` plus `process.memoryUsage()` logged on an interval.
Take an initial heap snapshot in Chrome DevTools (open `chrome://inspect`, attach to `node --inspect app.js`) and label it 'baseline'.
Exercise the suspected code path 50-100 times, force a GC (click the trash icon), then take a second snapshot labeled 'after'.
Switch the snapshot view to 'Comparison' and sort by '# Delta' — objects with a large positive delta that never drop are your retained leak.
Click a leaking object and read the 'Retainers' tree bottom-up to find what is holding the reference (often a closure, array, or event emitter).
Remove the reference: clear timers, call `removeListener`, bound array/cache size, or null out the closure variable.
Re-run the snapshot comparison to confirm the delta is now flat across iterations.
tips: Listeners added in a loop without removal are the #1 cause — watch for `MaxListenersExceededWarning`.
Module-level arrays and Maps live forever; never push to them without an eviction policy.

guides.title: Diagnose a growing-memory Python process
steps: Confirm it is the heap and not just OS-reserved memory: log `tracemalloc` totals, not just RSS from `top`.
Add `import tracemalloc; tracemalloc.start()` at startup and capture `tracemalloc.take_snapshot()` before and after the suspect loop.
Diff the snapshots with `snapshot2.compare_to(snapshot1, 'lineno')` and print the top 10 lines by size delta.
For reference cycles, run `gc.collect()` and inspect `gc.garbage`; if objects appear there they have `__del__` and uncollectable cycles.
Use `objgraph.show_growth()` to see which object types are accumulating between iterations.
Fix the retainer: break cycles with `weakref`, close files/sockets, or clear module-level caches and `functools.lru_cache` instances.
Re-snapshot to verify the per-iteration growth is gone.
tips: `lru_cache` with no `maxsize` grows unbounded — always set a limit.
Holding tracebacks (e.g. saving exceptions) keeps entire frames and their locals alive.

triggers: browser tab using too much memory
guides.title: Find a detached-DOM memory leak in the browser
steps: Open DevTools > Memory and take a heap snapshot after the page loads.
Interact with the feature that opens/closes views (modals, route changes) several times.
Take a second snapshot and type 'Detached' into the class filter — detached DOM trees still in memory are leaks.
Select a detached node and follow its retainers up to the JS reference keeping it alive.
Common culprit: an event listener or a stored DOM reference in a long-lived object/array — remove the listener on teardown and null the reference.
For frameworks, ensure cleanup runs (React `useEffect` return, Vue `onUnmounted`, removing `addEventListener` you added manually).
Repeat the snapshot cycle and confirm 'Detached' nodes no longer accumulate.
tips: `setInterval` that touches the DOM keeps the whole subtree alive — always `clearInterval` on unmount.
Global caches keyed by DOM elements leak; use `WeakMap` so the key can be GC'd.

guides.title: Speed up a slow SQL query
steps: Capture the exact query and run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (Postgres) or `EXPLAIN` (MySQL) to see the real plan and timings.
Look for `Seq Scan` / full table scans on large tables and high row estimates vs actual rows (stale stats).
Identify the columns used in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY and check whether a supporting index exists.
Add a targeted index (composite, column order matching filter then sort) and re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm an index scan replaces the seq scan.
Run `ANALYZE table` to refresh planner statistics if estimates were far off.
Reduce returned data: select only needed columns, add LIMIT, and avoid `SELECT *` that forces wide row fetches.
Re-measure end-to-end latency and confirm the plan cost dropped.
tips: A leading wildcard `LIKE '%foo'` cannot use a B-tree index — use trigram or full-text indexing instead.
Functions on indexed columns (`WHERE lower(email)=...`) disable the index unless you add a matching expression index.

guides.title: Eliminate an N+1 query problem
steps: Enable query logging (Django Debug Toolbar, Rails `log` / Bullet gem, or an ORM query counter) and load the slow page.
Count the queries: a repeated identical query that runs once per row of a parent list is the N+1 signature.
Identify the relationship being lazily loaded inside the loop or template.
Eager-load it: Django `select_related`/`prefetch_related`, Rails `includes`/`preload`, Sequelize `include`, Prisma `include`.
Reload and confirm the per-row queries collapse into one (or two) batched queries.
For aggregates, push the count/sum into the database with `annotate`/`group by` instead of looping in app code.
tips: `select_related` is a JOIN (one query); `prefetch_related` is a second query — use the right one for the relation type.
Serializers and template helpers can trigger hidden lazy loads — check those too, not just the controller.

guides.title: Analyze a JVM OutOfMemoryError / heap leak
steps: Run with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp` so a `.hprof` is written when it crashes.
Enable GC logging (`-Xlog:gc*`) and check whether pauses lengthen and old-gen never shrinks after Full GC — a true leak.
Open the heap dump in Eclipse MAT and run the 'Leak Suspects' report.
Inspect the 'Dominator Tree' to find the single object retaining the most heap.
Follow the GC roots path to the leak — frequently a static collection, ThreadLocal, or classloader retention.
Fix it: bound caches (Caffeine/`WeakHashMap`), remove `ThreadLocal` values after use, and avoid static `List`/`Map` accumulation.
Re-run under load with GC logs and confirm old-gen returns to baseline after collections.
tips: ThreadLocal in a thread pool leaks because pooled threads never die — always `remove()` in a finally block.
Don't just raise `-Xmx`; that hides leaks and delays the crash.

guides.title: Find what blocks the Node.js event loop
steps: Confirm symptom: requests queue up and latency spikes while CPU is pinned on one core.
Run with `node --prof app.js`, reproduce the load, then process the log with `node --prof-process isolate-*.log`.
Read the 'Summary' — a high percentage in JS/C++ ticks points to a hot synchronous function.
Search for synchronous APIs in hot paths: `fs.readFileSync`, `crypto.pbkdf2Sync`, large `JSON.parse`, big regex, or tight CPU loops.
Move heavy work off the loop: use async I/O, `worker_threads` for CPU work, or stream/chunk large parsing.
Add `--prof` again or use `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()` to verify event-loop lag has dropped.
tips: Catastrophic-backtracking regexes can block for seconds on one input — test patterns with adversarial strings.
`JSON.parse` on multi-MB payloads is synchronous; stream-parse large bodies.

guides.title: Fix excessive React re-renders
steps: Open React DevTools > Profiler, click record, interact, then stop and look at the flame graph for components rendering far more than expected.
Enable 'Highlight updates when components render' to visually spot components flashing on unrelated state changes.
Check why a component rendered (DevTools shows 'Why did this render?') — usually a new object/array/function prop created inline every render.
Memoize stable values with `useMemo`/`useCallback` and wrap pure children in `React.memo`.
Move state down so it doesn't re-render the whole tree, or lift context value into a memoized object.
Avoid recreating context values inline; provide a memoized value to prevent every consumer re-rendering.
Re-profile and confirm the render count for the hot components dropped.
tips: `React.memo` is useless if you pass a freshly-created object/function prop each render — memoize those too.
Don't over-memoize; the comparison cost can exceed the render for cheap components.

guides.title: Profile a Go program for memory and goroutine leaks
steps: Import `net/http/pprof` and expose it (`go func(){ http.ListenAndServe("localhost:6060", nil) }()`).
Check goroutine count over time: `curl localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=1` — a steadily rising count is a goroutine leak.
Capture a heap profile: `go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap`, then `top` and `list <func>` to find allocations.
For goroutine leaks, read the goroutine dump stacks to see where they're blocked (often a channel send/receive with no counterpart).
Fix leaked goroutines: add `context` cancellation, ensure channels get closed/drained, and avoid sending on a channel nobody reads.
Bound allocations: reuse buffers with `sync.Pool`, preallocate slices with `make([]T, 0, n)`, and avoid per-request large allocations.
Re-capture profiles under load and confirm goroutine count and heap stabilize.
tips: A goroutine blocked forever on a channel never gets GC'd — it and everything it references leak.
Use `-benchmem` with `go test -bench` to catch allocation regressions in hot functions.

guides.title: Profile and speed up slow Python code
steps: Get a coarse view first: `python -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py` and read the top functions by cumulative time.
Drill into the hottest function with line-level detail using `line_profiler` (`@profile` + `kernprof -l -v`).
Identify the real bottleneck — often a tight Python loop, repeated attribute lookups, or per-item I/O.
Vectorize numeric loops with NumPy/pandas, or move per-item I/O into a batch call.
Cache repeated pure computations with `functools.lru_cache` and hoist invariant work out of loops.
Re-run cProfile and confirm the cumulative time on the hot path dropped meaningfully.
tips: `cProfile` adds overhead and distorts micro-timings — trust relative ranking, not absolute numbers.
String concatenation in a loop is O(n²); build a list and `''.join()` instead.

guides.title: Diagnose a slow web page load
steps: Run Lighthouse (DevTools > Lighthouse) in an incognito window and note the LCP, TBT, and CLS scores plus the opportunities list.
Open the Network tab, reload with cache disabled, and sort by size and time to find large blocking resources.
Check the waterfall for render-blocking CSS/JS in the `<head>` and unoptimized images.
Defer/async non-critical scripts, inline critical CSS, and lazy-load below-the-fold images (`loading="lazy"`).
Compress and right-size assets: serve modern image formats (WebP/AVIF), enable gzip/brotli, and split large JS bundles.
Add caching headers and a CDN for static assets; preconnect/preload critical origins and fonts.
Re-run Lighthouse and confirm LCP and Total Blocking Time improved.
tips: The single biggest LCP win is usually optimizing the hero image (size + format + preload).
Third-party scripts (analytics, ads) often dominate TBT — audit them with the 'third-party usage' report.

guides.title: Resolve a container OOMKilled (exit code 137)
steps: Confirm the cause: `kubectl describe pod <pod>` shows `Reason: OOMKilled` and `Last State` with exit code 137.
Check the memory limit vs actual usage: `kubectl top pod` and compare to the `resources.limits.memory` in the spec.
Decide if it's a real leak or an under-provisioned limit by watching usage trend over time (monotonic climb = leak).
If it's a leak, profile the app inside the container (heap dump / pprof / tracemalloc) as you would normally.
If it's tuning, raise `limits.memory` and set `requests.memory` realistically; for the JVM add `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` so it respects cgroup limits.
Redeploy and monitor `kubectl top` and restart count to confirm the pod stays within budget.
tips: Older JVMs ignore container limits and size the heap to the host's RAM — use a container-aware JDK and `MaxRAMPercentage`.
Exit 137 = 128 + SIGKILL(9); it's the kernel OOM killer, not your app crashing.

guides.title: Fix Postgres connection exhaustion
steps: Confirm the error: app logs show `too many clients already` / `remaining connection slots are reserved`.
See who's connected: `SELECT count(*), state FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;` — many `idle in transaction` rows signal leaked connections.
Find leaks: connections in `idle in transaction` mean the app opened a transaction and never committed/rolled back or returned the connection.
Fix the app: ensure every borrowed connection is released in a `finally`, commit/rollback transactions promptly, and set a sane pool `max`.
Put a pooler in front (PgBouncer in transaction mode) so thousands of app connections multiplex onto few Postgres backends.
Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` so abandoned transactions get killed automatically.
Reload and watch `pg_stat_activity` to confirm idle-in-transaction count stays near zero.
tips: Each Postgres connection costs real RAM (~5-10MB) — pooling matters more than raising `max_connections`.
Serverless functions each open their own pool; use a shared pooler or you'll exhaust the DB instantly.

guides.title: Fix unbounded concurrency overwhelming a service
steps: Reproduce: a `Promise.all` over a large array fires thousands of requests at once, causing timeouts, ECONNRESET, or rate limits.
Confirm by logging the in-flight count or watching the downstream service's error rate spike at the moment the batch starts.
Replace the unbounded `Promise.all(items.map(fetch))` with a concurrency limiter (`p-limit`, a worker queue, or chunked batches).
Pick a sane concurrency (start at 5-10) based on the downstream's capacity, not the array size.
Add timeouts and retries-with-backoff so a slow downstream doesn't pile up requests.
Re-run the batch and confirm downstream error rate and latency stay flat.
tips: `Promise.allSettled` still launches everything at once — it only changes how rejections are reported, not concurrency.
Default Node HTTP keep-alive can cap sockets; tune the agent's `maxSockets` alongside your limiter.

triggers: why does my list stay full python
guides.title: Mutable default argument keeps old data
steps: Look for a function defined like def add(item, bag=[]) where the default is a list, dict, or set
Know that the default is created ONCE when Python reads the def line, not each call, so every call shares the same list
Change the default to None: def add(item, bag=None)
Inside the function add: if bag is None: bag = [] so a fresh list is made each call
Run the function twice in a row and confirm the second call starts empty
tips: This bites lists, dicts, and sets — anything that can be changed in place

triggers: items left behind after remove in loop
python deleting from list in for loop
guides.title: Removing items while looping over the same list
steps: Spot a for loop that calls my_list.remove() or del on the list it is looping over
Understand the loop's position jumps when items shift left, so it skips the next item
Loop over a copy instead: for item in my_list[:]: then remove from the original
Or build a new list with a comprehension: my_list = [x for x in my_list if keep(x)]
Run it and confirm every item you wanted gone is actually gone
tips: The [:] makes a shallow copy so the loop and the edits use different lists

triggers: why does is return false for equal values
guides.title: Using is instead of == for value checks
steps: Find a comparison using is, like if x is 5 or if name is 'Joe'
Know that is checks if two names point to the SAME object, not equal values
Switch to == when you mean 'has the same value': if x == 5
Keep is only for None checks: if x is None
Print x and the value you compare to, to confirm they truly match
Run again and verify the branch you expected now fires
tips: Small integers and short strings sometimes share objects, which makes is look like it works until it suddenly doesn't

guides.title: Decimal math gives a tiny error
steps: Print the result directly, e.g. print(0.1 + 0.2), and notice it shows 0.30000000000000004
Understand computers store decimals in binary so some values are slightly off
Stop comparing floats with ==
Use math.isclose(a, b) which returns True when two floats are nearly equal
If you need exact money math, switch to the decimal module: from decimal import Decimal
Run again and confirm the comparison now passes
tips: math.isclose is built for exactly this and reads cleanly

triggers: I named a variable list and it broke
guides.title: Variable name hides a built-in like list or str
steps: Read the error like 'list' object is not callable or 'str' object is not callable
Search your file for a variable named list, str, dict, sum, max, or id
Realize you replaced the built-in function with your own value
Rename your variable to something specific like word_list or total
Restart the program — the built-in is restored once the bad name is gone
Run again and confirm the built-in works
tips: Avoid naming variables after built-ins; pick descriptive names instead

triggers: global value stays the same python
guides.title: Function can't change an outside variable
steps: Notice a function assigns to a variable that also exists outside it
Understand that assigning inside a function makes a NEW local variable by default
If you truly must change the outer one, add global my_var at the top of the function
Better: return the new value and assign it where you call: count = bump(count)
Print the variable before and after the call to see if it actually changed
Run again and confirm the value updates
tips: Returning a value is cleaner and safer than using global

triggers: loop functions all return same value
lambda in loop wrong value python
guides.title: Functions made in a loop all use the last value
steps: Find a loop that builds functions or lambdas using the loop variable
Call them and notice they all return the loop's FINAL value
Understand the inner function looks up the variable when called, not when made
Capture the value with a default argument: lambda i=i: i inside the loop
Or use functools.partial to bind the current value
Run the made functions and confirm each gives its own value
tips: The default-argument trick (x=x) freezes the value at definition time

guides.title: list.sort() returned None
steps: Find a line like my_list = my_list.sort()
Understand .sort() sorts the list in place and returns None, so you erased your list
Remove the assignment: just call my_list.sort() on its own line
If you need a sorted copy and a return value, use sorted(my_list) instead
Print the list right after sorting to confirm it is ordered
Run again and verify the list is not None
tips: Methods that change a list in place (.sort, .reverse, .append) return None

triggers: can't delete from dict in loop
guides.title: Dictionary changed size during iteration
steps: Read the error: RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration
Find the loop that adds or deletes keys while looping over the same dict
Loop over a snapshot of the keys instead: for k in list(my_dict): then delete
Or build the keys to remove first, then delete them after the loop ends
Run it and confirm the right keys were removed
Verify the dict's final contents are correct
tips: Wrapping the keys in list() freezes them so edits during the loop are safe

guides.title: Step through code with the built-in debugger
steps: Add the line breakpoint() right where you want to pause
Run the program normally; it stops and shows a (Pdb) prompt at that line
Type n to run the next line, s to step into a function call
Type p variable_name to print any variable's current value
Type c to continue running until the next breakpoint or the end
Type q to quit the debugger when you have found the problem
tips: breakpoint() works in any modern Python without importing anything

triggers: cannot import name partially initialized module
guides.title: Circular import between two files
steps: Read the error: cannot import name X (most likely due to a circular import)
Notice file A imports file B and file B imports file A
Move the import inside the function that needs it instead of at the top of the file
Or pull the shared code into a third file that both import
Or import the module (import b) and use b.thing later, instead of from b import thing
Run again and confirm both files load
tips: A function-level import breaks the loop because it runs only when called

triggers: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces
guides.title: TabError — tabs and spaces mixed
steps: Read the error: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation
Open the file with whitespace shown so tabs and spaces look different
Pick spaces (the standard) for the whole file
Use your editor's 'convert tabs to spaces' command on the whole file
Re-check the flagged lines line up at the same column
Run again and confirm the TabError is gone
tips: Many editors have a one-click 'convert indentation to spaces' option

triggers: data not saved to file python
guides.title: Written data missing because the file wasn't closed
steps: Notice you wrote to a file but it looks empty when you read it
Find your open() call and check whether you ever close it
Switch to a with block: with open('f.txt', 'w') as f: f.write(text)
The with block closes the file automatically when it ends, flushing the data
Re-open the file to confirm the text is now saved
Run again and verify the content is present
tips: Always use 'with open(...)' so the file is closed and flushed for you

triggers: can't read file with special characters
guides.title: UnicodeDecodeError reading a file
steps: Read the error: it names a byte it could not decode
Find your open() call for reading
Tell Python the encoding explicitly: open('f.txt', encoding='utf-8')
If the file came from Windows, try encoding='cp1252' or 'latin-1'
If you only need raw bytes, open in binary mode 'rb' and decode yourself
Run again and confirm the file reads without error
tips: Always pass encoding='utf-8' when opening text files to avoid surprises

guides.title: JSONDecodeError parsing JSON
steps: Read the error: it gives a line and column where parsing failed
Print the raw text you passed to json.loads to see what is really there
Check for trailing commas, single quotes, or comments — JSON allows none of those
Confirm the text is not empty and is not actually HTML (like an error page)
If reading a file, use json.load(file_object), not json.loads(file_object)
Run again and confirm it parses
tips: json.load takes a file; json.loads takes a string — the s means string

triggers: csv row has wrong number of columns
csv split breaks on commas in field
guides.title: CSV columns split wrong
steps: Notice a row split into more pieces than there are columns
Suspect a comma inside a quoted field broke your manual line.split(',')
Stop splitting by hand — use the csv module: import csv
Read with csv.reader(file) which understands quotes correctly
If the file uses semicolons or tabs, pass delimiter=';' to csv.reader
Run again and confirm each row has the right number of fields
tips: The csv module handles quoted commas; a plain split never will

guides.title: Regex match returns None
steps: Print what re.search returned — None means no match was found
Print the exact string you searched so you can see hidden spaces or newlines
Test your pattern on a tiny known-good sample first
Remember to escape special characters like . and ( with a backslash, or use re.escape
Use a raw string for the pattern: r'\d+' so backslashes are literal
Run again and confirm the match object is not None before using .group()
tips: Always check 'if m:' before calling m.group() to avoid a crash on None

triggers: all objects share the same list python
guides.title: All instances share one list
steps: Notice changing one object's list also changes every other object's
Look at the class body — a list or dict defined directly there is shared by ALL instances
Move it into __init__: def __init__(self): self.items = []
Now each object gets its own fresh list when it is created
Make two objects, change one, and confirm the other is unchanged
Run again and verify they are independent
tips: Per-object data belongs in __init__, not in the class body

guides.title: Subclass missing parent setup
steps: Notice a child class is missing attributes the parent sets in __init__
Open the child's __init__ and check whether it calls the parent's
Add super().__init__(...) at the top of the child's __init__
Pass along any arguments the parent needs
Confirm the parent's attributes now exist on a child instance
Run again and verify the missing attributes appear
tips: When you write a child __init__, you usually need super().__init__() inside it

guides.title: Two equal-looking objects compare as not equal
steps: Notice obj_a == obj_b is False even though their data matches
Understand that by default Python compares object identity, not contents
Add an __eq__ method to your class comparing the fields you care about
Add a matching __hash__ if you also put the objects in sets or dict keys
Test: make two objects with the same data and confirm == now returns True
Run again and verify membership tests work
tips: If you define __eq__, define __hash__ too or the object becomes unhashable

guides.title: Printing an object shows a memory address
steps: Notice print(obj) shows something like <Dog object at 0x10f...>
Add a __repr__ method returning a useful string: return f'Dog(name={self.name!r})'
Use __repr__ for debugging output and __str__ for friendly user-facing text
Print the object again to confirm it shows real data
Lists of your objects will now print readably too
Run again and verify the output is informative
tips: __repr__ should ideally show how to recreate the object

triggers: map object empty after first use
guides.title: Generator is empty the second time you use it
steps: Notice a generator, map, or filter object works once then seems empty
Understand these are single-use — looping over them consumes them
If you need the values more than once, convert to a list first: data = list(gen)
Then loop over data as many times as you like
If memory matters and you must re-run, recreate the generator each time
Run again and confirm the second use has data
tips: map(), filter(), and zip() all return one-shot iterators in modern Python

guides.title: zip silently dropped extra items
steps: Notice zip stopped at the length of the SHORTEST input
Print the lengths of all the lists you zipped
If that truncation is wrong, decide what should happen to the extras
Use itertools.zip_longest(a, b, fillvalue=0) to pad the short ones
Or fix the upstream code so the lists end up the same length
Run again and confirm no items are silently lost
tips: zip pairs up to the shortest input; zip_longest pads instead

guides.title: Grouping into a dict the wrong way
steps: Notice a KeyError when you do my_dict[key].append(x) for a new key
The key does not exist yet, so there is nothing to append to
Use setdefault: my_dict.setdefault(key, []).append(x)
Or use a defaultdict: from collections import defaultdict; d = defaultdict(list)
With defaultdict(list) you can append to any key directly
Run again and confirm groups build without a KeyError
tips: defaultdict(list) is the cleanest way to group items by key

guides.title: A valid 0 or empty value is treated as missing
steps: Notice an if check skips when the value is 0, '', or an empty list
Understand 0, 0.0, '', [], {}, and None are all 'falsy' in Python
If you only meant to catch missing data, test explicitly: if x is None:
If you want to reject empty containers too, that may be fine — decide on purpose
Print the value and its type to confirm what it really is
Run again and confirm valid zeros are no longer skipped
tips: Use 'is None' when you specifically mean missing, so a real 0 still counts

guides.title: Comparison result is surprising
steps: Notice something like if a < b == c behaving oddly
Know Python chains comparisons: a < b < c means (a < b) and (b < c)
Avoid comparing a boolean to a number, like (a < b) < c, which compares True/False to a number
Add parentheses to make your intent explicit
Print the pieces separately to see each comparison's result
Run again and confirm the logic matches your intent
tips: Chained comparisons are handy but add parentheses when mixing operators

guides.title: and/or grouped differently than expected
steps: Notice a condition matches cases you did not intend
Remember and binds tighter than or, so a or b and c means a or (b and c)
Add parentheses to force your grouping: (a or b) and c
Print each sub-condition's True/False value with the inputs that surprised you
Adjust the parentheses until each test case behaves correctly
Run again and confirm the condition is right
tips: When mixing and with or, always add parentheses to be sure

guides.title: Comprehension result is empty or wrong
steps: Print the comprehension's output to see if it is empty or has the wrong items
Check the condition at the end (if ...) is not filtering everything out
Confirm the source you iterate over actually has items at that point
Watch for a one-shot iterator as the source — list it first if reused
Break a complex comprehension into a plain for loop to debug it step by step
Run again and confirm the contents are correct
tips: When a comprehension confuses you, rewrite it as a normal loop to see what happens

triggers: break only exits inner loop python
how to break out of two loops
guides.title: break only exits the inner loop
steps: Notice break stops the inner loop but the outer loop keeps going
Understand break only leaves the single loop it is in
Move the work into a function and use return to exit both loops at once
Or set a flag, break the inner loop, then check the flag to break the outer
Or use a for/else with a sentinel value to detect the early exit
Run again and confirm both loops stop when intended
tips: Wrapping nested loops in a function lets one return exit them all

guides.title: continue in a while loop skips the counter update
steps: Notice a while loop hangs after you added continue
Find the counter increment (like i += 1) and check it comes AFTER continue
Understand continue jumps back to the top, skipping any code below it
Move the increment ABOVE the continue, or convert to a for loop with range
Print the counter each pass to confirm it now advances
Run again and confirm the loop ends
tips: In a while loop, update the counter before any continue statement

triggers: default time stays the same python
guides.title: Default argument value is frozen at definition time
steps: Notice a default like def log(t=time.time()) always shows the same time
Understand the default is computed ONCE when the def line runs, not per call
Set the default to None instead: def log(t=None)
Inside the function: if t is None: t = time.time()
Call it twice with a pause and confirm the times now differ
Run again and verify the default is fresh each call
tips: Any 'live' default (time, random, empty list) must be built inside the function

guides.title: Random results change every run, blocking debugging
steps: Notice a bug that only happens sometimes because random values differ each run
Temporarily set a seed at the top: import random; random.seed(42)
Now the same 'random' sequence repeats every run so you can reproduce the bug
Debug with the fixed seed until the issue is found and fixed
Remove or randomize the seed again before shipping
Run a few times to confirm the fix holds across different seeds
tips: A fixed seed turns a flaky bug into a repeatable one you can actually catch

guides.title: time.sleep freezes the whole program
steps: Notice nothing else happens while time.sleep is running
Understand sleep blocks the entire thread until it finishes
If you only meant a short pause, that is fine — confirm the duration is right
If other work must continue, use threading or asyncio instead of sleeping in the main flow
For a countdown, sleep in small steps and print progress between them
Run again and confirm the timing behaves as intended
tips: time.sleep stops everything; use it only when a full pause is what you want

guides.title: A bare except is hiding the real error
steps: Find a try block ending in except: pass or a bare except
Understand it silences EVERY error, including bugs you needed to see
Temporarily change it to except Exception as e: print(e) to reveal what is happening
Catch only the specific error you expect, like except ValueError
Never use a bare 'except:' — it even catches Ctrl+C
Run again and read the now-visible error message
tips: Catch the narrowest exception you can; print it while debugging

guides.title: except clause doesn't catch the error
steps: Notice the program still crashes despite a try/except around it
Read the traceback to see the ACTUAL error type raised
Compare it to the type in your except clause — they probably differ
Change the except to match, or list several: except (ValueError, TypeError)
Confirm the error is even raised inside the try block, not before or after it
Run again and confirm the exception is caught
tips: The except type must match (or be a parent of) the error that is actually raised

triggers: return value wrong with finally python
guides.title: finally block changed the return value
steps: Notice a function returns the wrong value when it has a finally block
Check whether the finally block itself has a return statement
Understand a return in finally OVERRIDES any earlier return or exception
Remove the return from finally; use it only for cleanup like closing files
Move the real return outside the try/finally if needed
Run again and confirm the correct value comes back
tips: Keep finally for cleanup only — never put a return inside it

guides.title: Unexpected behavior from for/else
steps: Notice the else block after a for or while loop runs when you did not expect it
Understand loop-else runs when the loop finishes WITHOUT hitting break
If you wanted else to run only on a missing item, that is correct — confirm your break fires
If you misread it as a normal if-else, remove the else and rethink the logic
Add a print in both the break path and the else to see which runs
Run again and confirm the flow matches your intent
tips: Loop-else means 'the loop never broke', which surprises almost everyone

guides.title: Assertions are being skipped
steps: Notice an assert that should fail does nothing
Check whether Python was started with the -O flag, which strips all asserts
Understand asserts are for internal checks during development, not for real validation
For input you must always validate, use an if + raise instead of assert
Run without -O to confirm the assert works during debugging
Run again and verify the check fires as expected
