tips: Never rely on assert for security or user-input checks — it can be turned off

triggers: my file has no attribute python
named file same as module python
guides.title: Your file name hides a standard module
steps: Read an odd error like module 'random' has no attribute 'randint'
Check whether YOUR file is named the same as the module (random.py, json.py, etc.)
Python imported your file instead of the real library
Rename your file to something unique like my_random.py
Delete any leftover .pyc cache or __pycache__ folder
Run again and confirm the real module loads
tips: Never name your script the same as a library you import

guides.title: Old code keeps running after edits
steps: Notice your changes seem to have no effect
Confirm you are running and editing the SAME file (check the path)
Delete the __pycache__ folder and any .pyc files to clear stale bytecode
Make sure you saved the file before running
If using a notebook or REPL, restart it so it re-imports fresh
Run again and confirm the new code runs
tips: A long-running REPL or notebook keeps old imports until you restart it

guides.title: Notebook variable has a stale value
steps: Notice a variable in your notebook holds a value no cell currently sets
Realize cells can run out of order, leaving leftover state
Use Restart Kernel to wipe all variables
Then Run All Cells from the top in order
Confirm the suspicious variable now has the expected value
Re-run your test cell to verify the result
tips: Restart and Run All catches bugs hidden by out-of-order cell execution

triggers: prints out of order with logs
guides.title: Print output appears late or out of order
steps: Notice prints show up all at once or after later output
Understand output is buffered, so it may not appear immediately
Force it out: print(msg, flush=True)
Or run Python with the -u flag for unbuffered output
If mixing print with logging, the buffering can reorder them — pick one channel
Run again and confirm the output order is correct
tips: print(..., flush=True) forces the line out right away

guides.title: Type hints didn't stop a wrong type
steps: Notice a wrong type slipped through even though you wrote a type hint
Understand Python does NOT check type hints at runtime — they are documentation
To catch type mismatches, run a checker like mypy on your code
For runtime safety, add an explicit isinstance check and raise a clear error
Print the actual type at the function start while debugging: print(type(x))
Run the checker and confirm it flags the mismatch
tips: Hints help tools and readers, but only mypy/pyright actually check them

triggers: nested list copy still linked python
guides.title: Copy didn't separate nested lists
steps: Notice editing an INNER list in your copy also changes the original
Understand .copy() and list[:] are shallow — they share the inner objects
Import copy and use copy.deepcopy(original) for a fully independent copy
Edit the inner list of the deep copy and confirm the original is untouched
Use deepcopy only when needed — it is slower for big structures
Run again and verify the nested data is separate
tips: Shallow copies duplicate the outer container but share what's inside it

guides.title: Reverse slice returns nothing
steps: Notice a slice with a negative step came back empty
Understand with a negative step the start must be HIGHER than the stop
For a full reverse, leave start and stop blank: my_list[::-1]
Avoid mixing positive bounds with a negative step unless you mean it
Print the slice result to confirm it has items
Run again and verify the reversed slice is correct
tips: my_list[::-1] is the clean way to reverse anything sliceable

guides.title: startswith with multiple options fails
steps: Notice text.startswith(['a', 'b']) raised a TypeError
Understand startswith accepts a string or a TUPLE of strings, not a list
Pass a tuple: text.startswith(('a', 'b'))
The same rule applies to endswith
Test with a value that should match one of the options
Run again and confirm it returns True for matches
tips: Use a tuple, not a list, with startswith and endswith

guides.title: Hand-built file path breaks across systems
steps: Notice a path like 'folder\\file.txt' fails on a different operating system
Stop gluing paths with slashes by hand
Use pathlib: from pathlib import Path; p = Path('folder') / 'file.txt'
Path picks the right separator automatically for the system
Use os.path.join as an older alternative if needed
Run again and confirm the path works on your system
tips: pathlib's / operator builds correct paths on every platform

triggers: file works from one folder not another python
script can't find file when run elsewhere
guides.title: File found from one folder but not another
steps: Notice the program finds a file when run from its own folder but not elsewhere
Understand relative paths are based on the current working directory, not the script's location
To anchor paths to the script, use Path(__file__).parent
Build the path from there: Path(__file__).parent / 'data.txt'
Print that resolved path to confirm it points where you expect
Run again from a different folder to confirm it still works
tips: Path(__file__).parent gives the folder the script lives in, regardless of where you run it

guides.title: subprocess command not found
steps: Notice subprocess.run failed to find the command
Pass the command as a LIST of parts: ['ls', '-l'], not one big string
If you really need shell features, set shell=True and pass a single string
Print the exact command list to confirm there are no stray spaces
Capture output to see the real error: subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True)
Run again and read the captured stderr if it still fails
tips: A list of arguments avoids quoting headaches and is safer than shell=True

triggers: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes
guides.title: Can't compare naive and aware datetimes
steps: Read the error: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes
Understand one datetime has a timezone and the other does not
Pick one style for the whole program — usually timezone-aware in UTC
Make aware times with datetime.now(timezone.utc)
Convert a naive time by attaching a tz, or strip the tz if you truly mean local-naive
Run again and confirm the comparison works
tips: Pick aware-UTC everywhere and convert at the edges to avoid mixing

triggers: time data does not match format python
guides.title: Date string won't parse with strptime
steps: Read the error: time data 'X' does not match format 'Y'
Compare the format string to the actual text character by character
Match separators exactly: use %Y-%m-%d for 2026-05-29, %d/%m/%Y for 29/05/2026
Use %H:%M:%S for time, and watch %m (month) versus %M (minute)
Strip stray spaces from the input before parsing
Run again and confirm it parses
tips: %m is month and %M is minute — mixing them is a classic slip

guides.title: Find which part of the code is slow
steps: Wrap a suspect section with timing: import time; start=time.perf_counter() ... print(time.perf_counter()-start)
Run and note which section takes the most time
For a fuller picture, run python -m cProfile your_script.py
Read the profile output sorted by cumulative time to find the hot spot
Focus your fix on that one slow part, not the whole program
Re-measure after the fix to confirm it is faster
tips: Measure before optimizing — the slow part is often not where you guessed

triggers: program uses more and more ram
guides.title: Memory keeps growing over time
steps: Notice memory usage climbing the longer the program runs
Look for a list, dict, or cache that you keep appending to but never clear
Print its len() periodically to confirm it grows without bound
Cap it: keep only the last N items, or clear it when done with a batch
For caching, use functools.lru_cache(maxsize=...) which evicts old entries
Run again and confirm memory levels off
tips: An ever-growing global list or cache is the usual memory hog

guides.title: Building a giant list runs out of memory
steps: Notice a MemoryError or huge memory use when building a big list
Ask whether you ever need ALL items at once, or process them one at a time
If one at a time, use a generator: replace [x for x in src] with (x for x in src)
Read big files line by line: for line in file_object, not file.readlines()
Process and discard each item instead of storing them all
Run again and confirm memory stays low
tips: Generators yield one item at a time, so they never hold the whole list

guides.title: Threads don't speed up CPU work
steps: Notice adding threads did not make CPU-heavy work faster
Understand the Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread run Python at a time
Threads help with WAITING work (network, disk), not pure CPU math
For CPU-bound work, use multiprocessing instead of threading
Split the work across processes with concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor
Re-measure and confirm the CPU work now scales
tips: Threads for I/O waiting; processes for CPU crunching

guides.title: Shared counter gives wrong totals with threads
steps: Notice a counter updated by several threads ends up with the wrong total
Understand count += 1 is not atomic — threads can interleave and lose updates
Protect the update with a lock: with my_lock: count += 1
Create one lock shared by all the threads
Or have each thread return its own total and sum them at the end
Run again several times and confirm the total is now correct
tips: Even count += 1 needs a lock when multiple threads touch it

guides.title: Coroutine was never awaited
steps: Read the warning: coroutine 'X' was never awaited
Find where you called an async function without await
Add await before the call: result = await fetch()
Confirm the calling function is itself async (defined with async def)
Run the top-level coroutine with asyncio.run(main())
Run again and confirm the warning is gone and you get a real result
tips: Calling an async function without await just makes a coroutine object, not a result

guides.title: A blocking call freezes the async event loop
steps: Notice your async program stalls and other tasks stop progressing
Look for a blocking call like time.sleep or a heavy synchronous request
Replace time.sleep with await asyncio.sleep so the loop can run other tasks
For unavoidable blocking work, run it in a thread with asyncio.to_thread
Confirm awaits surround anything that waits
Run again and confirm tasks now overlap
tips: Inside async code, use await asyncio.sleep, never time.sleep

triggers: bool of string always true python
guides.title: bool('False') is surprisingly True
steps: Notice bool('False') or bool('0') returns True
Understand any NON-EMPTY string is truthy, regardless of its contents
Do not use bool() to turn text into a real True/False
Compare explicitly: value == 'True', or check a set of accepted words
For config flags, map strings: text.strip().lower() in ('1','true','yes')
Run again and confirm the flag is read correctly
tips: Only an empty string is falsy; the word 'False' is still truthy

triggers: all returns true on empty python
guides.title: all() on an empty list is True
steps: Notice all([]) returns True and any([]) returns False, which surprised you
Understand these are the defined edge cases for empty input
If an empty collection should NOT pass your check, test for it first
Add: if not items: handle the empty case before calling all/any
Confirm your logic with both an empty and a non-empty input
Run again and verify both cases behave correctly
tips: all() of nothing is vacuously True; check for empty when that matters

triggers: TypeError comparing str and int sort
sorting list with numbers and text
guides.title: Sorting a mixed-type list crashes
steps: Read the error: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'
Print the list and notice it mixes numbers and text
Decide on one comparison basis for everything
Sort by a key that normalizes types, e.g. key=str to compare as text
Or clean the data so it is all one type before sorting
Run again and confirm the sort completes
tips: A key= function lets you sort items by a consistent derived value

guides.title: Deep dictionary access crashes on a missing level
steps: Read the KeyError naming which level was missing
Notice a chain like data['a']['b']['c'] crashes if any level is absent
Print each level one at a time to find where it breaks
Use chained .get with defaults: data.get('a', {}).get('b', {}).get('c')
For deeply nested config, consider a small helper that walks the keys safely
Run again and confirm the missing level returns a default instead of crashing
tips: Chaining .get with {} defaults lets deep access fail soft

guides.title: Function unexpectedly changed the caller's list
steps: Notice a list you passed in got modified after the function ran
Understand lists and dicts are passed by reference, so edits affect the original
If the function should not alter the input, work on a copy inside it: data = data.copy()
If the change is intended, document it clearly so callers expect it
Test by printing the original list before and after the call
Run again and confirm the original is preserved when it should be
tips: Copy a mutable argument inside the function when callers shouldn't see your edits

triggers: a bytes-like object is required not str
can't mix str and bytes python
guides.title: Mixing bytes and text
steps: Read the error: a bytes-like object is required, not 'str' (or the reverse)
Recall network and file-binary data is bytes (b'...'), and regular text is str
Decode bytes to text: data.decode('utf-8')
Encode text to bytes: text.encode('utf-8')
Pick one type for the section of code and convert at the boundary
Run again and confirm the types match
tips: bytes carry a b prefix; decode to text and encode back to bytes

triggers: second loop over file empty python
guides.title: Second loop over a file reads nothing
steps: Notice a second 'for line in file' loop reads no lines
Understand a file object is an iterator — the first loop consumed it
Seek back to the start: file.seek(0) before the second loop
Or read into a list once: lines = file.readlines() and loop over that
Confirm the second pass now has data
Run again and verify both loops process the lines
tips: A file is read once unless you seek(0) or store the lines

triggers: type check fails for subclass python
guides.title: Type check misbehaves with subclasses
steps: Notice a type check passed or failed unexpectedly, e.g. a bool counted as an int
Understand bool is a SUBCLASS of int, so isinstance(True, int) is True
Use isinstance for normal checks since it respects subclasses
Use type(x) is int only when you must EXCLUDE subclasses
Decide which behavior you actually want and pick accordingly
Run again and confirm the check matches your intent
tips: isinstance respects subclasses; 'type(x) is C' demands an exact match

guides.title: Method chain breaks because one step returns None
steps: Read where in the chain the AttributeError on NoneType happens
Identify which method returns None — often an in-place one like .sort or .append
Split the chain into separate lines so you can inspect each step's result
Replace the in-place method with one that returns a value (sort -> sorted)
Re-chain only the steps that return usable values
Run again and confirm the chain works
tips: In-place methods return None, so they can't sit in the middle of a chain

guides.title: Line continuation joined lines unexpectedly
steps: Notice two lines behaved as if joined, or code after them seemed ignored
Check for a stray backslash at the end of a line, which continues it
Check for an unclosed bracket, paren, or quote that swallows the next line
Close the bracket or remove the backslash so the statement ends where you intend
Re-indent and re-read the block to confirm structure
Run again and confirm each statement is separate
tips: An unclosed ( [ { silently merges the next lines into one statement

triggers: triple quote string has extra spaces python
guides.title: Multi-line string has unwanted indentation
steps: Print the triple-quoted string and notice leading spaces on each line
Understand the indentation in your code becomes part of the string
Dedent it with textwrap.dedent and a leading backslash to drop the first newline
Or move the string to the left margin despite breaking visual nesting
Or build lines in a list and join with newlines
Run again and confirm the string has no stray indentation
tips: textwrap.dedent removes the common leading whitespace from every line

triggers: only last item saved to file python
guides.title: Only the last item ended up in the file
steps: Notice the output file holds only the final item from a loop
Check whether you open the file with mode 'w' INSIDE the loop each pass
Each 'w' open truncates the file, erasing previous writes
Open the file ONCE before the loop and write inside it
Or open in append mode 'a' if you must reopen each time
Run again and confirm all items are saved
tips: Open the file once outside the loop, then write each item inside

guides.title: input() raises EOFError
steps: Read the error: EOFError: EOF when reading a line
Understand there was no input available — common when input is piped or redirected
Confirm whether the program is meant to run interactively
Wrap input in try/except EOFError to handle the no-input case gracefully
If reading piped data, read from sys.stdin instead of calling input repeatedly
Run again and confirm it handles missing input
tips: Piped or empty input gives no line to read, raising EOFError

triggers: can't stop program with ctrl c python
guides.title: Ctrl+C won't stop the program
steps: Notice pressing Ctrl+C does nothing
Look for a bare 'except:' that is catching KeyboardInterrupt and ignoring it
Change it to catch a specific exception so Ctrl+C passes through
If you intentionally handle KeyboardInterrupt, make sure it actually exits
Check no tight C-level loop or sleep is swallowing the signal
Run again and confirm Ctrl+C stops the program
tips: A bare except even catches Ctrl+C — always catch specific exceptions

guides.title: lru_cache fails on a list argument
steps: Read the error: unhashable type: 'list'
Understand cached functions need hashable (unchangeable) arguments
Lists, dicts, and sets are not hashable, so they can't be cache keys
Convert a list argument to a tuple before calling: cached_fn(tuple(items))
Or design the function to take a tuple in the first place
Run again and confirm the cache works
tips: Tuples are hashable; lists are not — convert before caching

guides.title: Recursive function leaks results between calls
steps: Notice a recursive function's results pile up across separate top-level calls
Check for a mutable default accumulator like def walk(node, acc=[])
That single shared list survives between calls, mixing results
Default acc to None and create a fresh list when it is None
Or return new lists and combine them instead of mutating a shared one
Run two separate calls and confirm results no longer leak
tips: Recursion with a mutable default accumulator is a classic leak

triggers: Decimal still has rounding error python
guides.title: Decimal still shows a float error
steps: Notice Decimal(0.1) shows a long imprecise tail
Understand you fed it a float that was ALREADY imprecise
Build Decimal from a STRING instead: Decimal('0.1')
Now the decimal value is exact as written
Use Decimal for money calculations throughout that section
Run again and confirm the value is exact
tips: Always pass Decimal a string, never a float, to keep precision

triggers: exception variable gone after except python
guides.title: Exception variable is gone after the except block
steps: Notice using the exception name after the except block raises NameError
Understand 'except E as e' deletes e when the block ends, by design
If you need the error later, save it: error = e inside the block
Then use the saved variable outside the block
Confirm by printing the saved value after the try
Run again and verify the error info survives
tips: The 'as e' name is cleared when the except block finishes

guides.title: A calculation produced nan or inf
steps: Notice a value shows as nan (not a number) or inf (infinity)
Trace it back: nan often comes from 0.0/0.0 or sqrt of a negative float
inf often comes from dividing by a tiny number or overflow in float math
Check for nan with math.isnan(x), since nan != nan is always True
Guard the operation that produced it, or clean the input data
Run again and confirm the value is a normal number
tips: nan is never equal to anything, even itself — use math.isnan to detect it

triggers: argparse argument is string not int python
command line number is text python
guides.title: Command-line number arrives as text
steps: Notice a command-line argument behaves like text in math
Understand argparse gives strings unless you tell it the type
Add type=int (or type=float) to the add_argument call
Confirm with print(type(args.count)) after parsing
Re-run with a sample value and check the math works
Run again and verify the conversion happened
tips: Pass type=int to add_argument so argparse converts for you

triggers: files processed in wrong order python
guides.title: Files processed in an unpredictable order
steps: Notice os.walk or os.listdir returns files in no particular order
Understand the order depends on the filesystem and is not guaranteed
If order matters, sort the names yourself: for name in sorted(files)
For natural numeric order (file2 before file10), sort with a numeric key
Print the order to confirm it is now predictable
Run again and verify the processing order is stable
tips: Never rely on directory listing order — sort it yourself when it matters

guides.title: The original error got hidden by a new one
steps: Notice the traceback shows a new error but not the one that really started it
Look in your except block for code that raises a fresh exception
Preserve the cause: raise NewError(...) from original_error
Or just re-raise the original with a bare raise to keep its traceback
Print or log the original error before raising the new one
Run again and confirm both errors appear in the traceback
tips: 'raise X from e' keeps the original cause visible in the traceback

triggers: log message wrong with formatting python
guides.title: Log message formatting evaluated even when hidden
steps: Notice an f-string in a debug log runs expensive work even when debug is off
Understand an f-string is built BEFORE logging decides to show it
Use logging's lazy form: logging.debug('value %s', expensive())
Wait — that still calls expensive(); guard heavy work with logger.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG)
For simple values, the %s lazy form avoids building the string when hidden
Run again and confirm the heavy work is skipped when debug is off
tips: Pass values as logging args (%s) so the string is built only if it will be shown

guides.title: Saved dict keys reflect later changes
steps: Notice a saved my_dict.keys() seemed to change after you edited the dict
Understand .keys(), .values(), and .items() are LIVE views, not snapshots
To freeze them, wrap in list: saved = list(my_dict.keys())
Use the frozen list when you need a stable copy
Confirm by editing the dict and checking the saved list is unchanged
Run again and verify the snapshot stays put
tips: Wrap a dict view in list() to take a real snapshot

triggers: map result not a list python
guides.title: map result prints as an object
steps: Notice print(map(...)) shows something like <map object at 0x...>
Understand map returns a lazy iterator, not a list
Wrap it in list() to materialize: result = list(map(fn, items))
Or loop over it directly with for x in map(fn, items)
Remember it is single-use, so list it if you need it more than once
Run again and confirm you see the values
tips: map is lazy; call list() on it to see or reuse the values

triggers: a = b = list both change python
guides.title: Chained assignment made two names share a list
steps: Notice a = b = [] then editing one changes both
Understand chained assignment binds BOTH names to the SAME single list
To get two independent lists, assign separately: a = []; b = []
For nested copies, use copy.deepcopy as needed
Edit one and confirm the other is unchanged
Run again and verify they are independent
tips: a = b = [] creates one list with two names, not two lists

triggers: bool key collides with int key
guides.title: Dict keys 1 and True collide
steps: Notice a dict lost an entry where you used both 1 and True as keys
Understand True == 1 and False == 0, and equal keys collide in a dict
The later assignment overwrites the earlier one
Use distinct key types or values so they don't compare equal
Print the dict to confirm which key survived
Run again and verify the keys you need are present
tips: True is treated as 1 and False as 0 for dict keys and sets

triggers: deep recursion crash large input python
guides.title: Deep recursion crashes on large input
steps: Notice the program crashes with RecursionError only on big inputs
Understand Python limits recursion depth (around 1000) to protect the stack
If the logic is correct but the input is deep, rewrite it as a loop with an explicit stack
Use a list as a stack: push work to do, pop and process until empty
Avoid raising the recursion limit unless you fully understand the risk
Run with the large input and confirm it completes
tips: Convert deep recursion to an iterative loop with your own stack list

triggers: can't add list to set python
guides.title: Can't put a list into a set
steps: Read the error: unhashable type: 'list'
Understand sets and dict keys need hashable, unchangeable items
Lists, dicts, and sets are mutable, so they can't go inside a set
Convert inner lists to tuples: my_set.add(tuple(items))
Use frozenset if you need a set inside a set
Run again and confirm the items are accepted
tips: Tuples and frozensets are hashable; lists, dicts, and sets are not

guides.title: assert with a comma always passes
steps: Notice an assert never fails even when it should
Look for a comma: assert x == 5, 'message' is correct, but assert (x == 5, 'message') is a bug
The second form asserts a non-empty TUPLE, which is always truthy
Remove the parentheses so the message is the assert's second argument
Re-test with a value that should fail to confirm it now fails
Run again and verify the assert works
tips: assert condition, message — never wrap them in parentheses together

triggers: literal curly brace in f-string python
guides.title: Need a literal curly brace in a format string
steps: Notice an f-string or .format crashes or eats your braces
To show a literal { write {{ and for } write }}
Example: f'{{not a slot}} {value}' prints {not a slot} then the value
Check each brace is paired correctly after doubling
Print a sample to confirm the literal braces appear
Run again and verify the output is right
tips: Double the braces — {{ and }} — to show literal curly brackets

guides.title: Instance attribute hides a method of the same name
steps: Read an error like 'int' object is not callable when calling self.count()
Search for self.count = something that set an attribute with the method's name
Realize the attribute now shadows the method on that instance
Rename either the method or the attribute so they differ
Restart and confirm the method is reachable again
Run again and verify the call works
tips: Don't give an instance attribute the same name as a method

guides.title: Dataclass rejects a mutable default
steps: Read the error: mutable default for field X is not allowed
Understand dataclasses block list/dict/set defaults to prevent the shared-default bug
Use field(default_factory=list): items: list = field(default_factory=list)
Import field from dataclasses
Now each instance gets its own fresh list
Run again and confirm two instances have separate lists
tips: default_factory=list gives each dataclass instance its own list

triggers: builtin replaced by import star python
guides.title: A star import overwrote a built-in
steps: Notice a built-in like sum or max suddenly behaves differently
Look for a from module import * that may have pulled in a same-named function
Understand star imports can silently shadow built-ins and other names
Replace the star import with explicit names: from module import only_what_you_need
Restart so the built-ins are restored
Run again and confirm the built-in works as expected
tips: Avoid 'from x import *' — it can silently overwrite names you rely on

triggers: extra blank lines csv windows python
guides.title: Extra blank lines appear in written output
steps: Notice every other line is blank, often when writing CSV on Windows
Understand the csv module already adds line endings, and text mode may add more
Open the file with newline='' when using the csv module: open(path, 'w', newline='')
For plain text, make sure you are not adding '\n' that the file mode also translates
Re-open the file and confirm the blank lines are gone
Run again and verify clean output
tips: Pass newline='' to open() when writing CSV to avoid doubled line breaks

triggers: id changed for same object python
guides.title: Confused by id() values changing or repeating
steps: Notice id() gives the same number for different objects, or changes for one
Understand id is only the object's address while it LIVES; freed addresses get reused
Don't use id to track object equality or identity over time
To check if two names point to the same live object, use 'is'
To compare contents, use == (and define __eq__ for your classes)
Run again using the right operator and confirm the result
tips: id values are reused after objects die — never use them as long-lived keys

triggers: module code runs on import python
guides.title: Importing a module ran code unexpectedly
steps: Notice code ran (or printed) just by importing a module
Understand everything at the top level of a module runs ON import
Move runnable code into functions so importing does nothing on its own
Guard the script's main action with: if __name__ == '__main__':
Now the code runs only when the file is executed directly, not when imported
Run both ways and confirm the import is now side-effect-free
tips: Wrap a script's actions in 'if __name__ == "__main__":' so importing stays quiet

guides.title: Custom exception isn't caught where expected
steps: Notice a try/except for your custom exception doesn't catch it
Check whether two different files define same-named exception classes
Understand a class from one import is NOT the same class as another import
Make sure you import the exception from the SAME place you raise it
Print the actual exception's class and module to compare
Run again and confirm the except now catches it
tips: Two classes with the same name from different modules are different types

triggers: how to add timeout to loop python
guides.title: Add a safety limit to a loop that might run forever
steps: Identify a loop whose ending condition you are not 100% sure about
Add a max-iteration guard: for _ in range(1000000): or a counter that breaks
Inside, break when the real condition is met
If the guard trips, print a warning so you know it ran too long
This turns a hang into a clear, debuggable stop
Run and confirm the loop either finishes or warns instead of hanging
tips: A max-iteration guard converts silent hangs into visible, fixable stops

triggers: program behaves differently with optimization python
guides.title: Important logic hidden inside an assert disappears
steps: Notice a behavior changes when Python runs with the -O flag
Search for an assert that does real work, like assert do_setup()
Understand asserts are stripped under -O, so that work never runs
Move the real logic out of the assert onto its own line
Keep asserts purely for checking conditions, with no side effects
Run with -O and confirm the behavior is now consistent
tips: Never put real work inside an assert — it vanishes when optimizations are on

triggers: float not found in set python
guides.title: Float lookups in a set or dict miss
steps: Notice a float you expect is not found in a set or as a dict key
Understand tiny rounding differences make two 'equal-looking' floats unequal
Don't use raw floats as set members or dict keys when precision varies
Round to a fixed number of decimals before using as a key: round(x, 4)
Or store an integer count of the smallest unit (like cents) instead
Run again and confirm lookups now hit
tips: Round floats to a fixed precision before using them as keys or set members

triggers: inner function can't change outer variable
guides.title: Inner function can't update the enclosing variable
steps: Notice an inner (nested) function fails to change a variable from the function around it
Understand assigning inside the inner function makes a new local by default
Add nonlocal count at the top of the inner function to target the enclosing one
Reserve global for module-level variables; use nonlocal for enclosing-function ones
Print the variable after calling the inner function to confirm the change
Run again and verify the update sticks
tips: nonlocal targets the nearest enclosing function's variable; global targets the module's

guides.title: Event listener firing more than once
steps: Add a console.log with a counter inside the handler to confirm how many times it runs
Check whether addEventListener is called inside a function that runs more than once (like a render or a loop)
Look for the same handler attached in both HTML (onclick) and JS (addEventListener)
Move the addEventListener call to a spot that only runs one time, like top-level setup
If you must attach inside a re-running function, call removeEventListener with the same function reference first
Re-test by clicking once and confirming the counter goes up by exactly one
tips: A named function lets you removeEventListener later; an inline arrow function cannot be removed because you lost the reference

guides.title: Assignment to constant variable error
steps: Read the error to find which variable name it complains about
Find where that variable was declared with const
Decide if the value really needs to change; if yes, change const to let
If it should never change, find the line trying to reassign it and remove or fix that line
Remember you CAN still change the inside of a const object or array, just not point it at a new value
Re-run and confirm the error is gone
tips: const protects the binding, not the contents: const arr = []; arr.push(1) is fine, arr = [1] is not

triggers: async function returns promise instead of value
why is my value a Promise
guides.title: Async function gives a Promise instead of the value
steps: Notice that calling an async function always returns a Promise, never the plain value
Find where you used the result and check if you forgot await
Add await in front of the async call, and make sure the surrounding function is also async
If you cannot use await, use .then(value => { ... }) to read the result inside the callback
Log the value AFTER awaiting, not before
Re-run and confirm you now see the real value, not Promise { <pending> }
tips: await only works inside an async function or at the top level of a module

guides.title: await inside forEach does not pause the loop
steps: Confirm the symptom: code after the forEach runs before the awaited work finishes
Understand that forEach ignores the Promise your async callback returns
Switch to a plain for...of loop, which respects await
Put your await statements inside the for...of body
If you want them to run at the same time, collect Promises in an array and use await Promise.all
Re-run and confirm the order of logs is now correct
tips: for...of waits one at a time; Promise.all runs them together and is faster when order does not matter

guides.title: JSON.parse throws unexpected token
steps: Read the error; the position number points at the bad character
console.log the exact string you are parsing right before JSON.parse
Check it is real JSON: double quotes only, no trailing comma, no JS comments
If it came from fetch, you may have HTML (an error page) instead of JSON; log it to see
If the string is already an object, you do not need JSON.parse at all
Fix the source so it sends valid JSON, then re-run
tips: A response that starts with < is almost always an HTML error page, not JSON

guides.title: Fetch data shows up as undefined
steps: Remember fetch is asynchronous, so the data is not ready on the next line
Use await on fetch, then await on response.json()
Confirm you returned or assigned the parsed value, not the Promise
Log the data right after the second await
Check the Network tab to confirm the request actually returned a body
Re-run and confirm the data is now defined
tips: fetch needs two awaits: one for the response, one for response.json()

guides.title: Request blocked by CORS in the browser
steps: Read the console message; it names the origin that was blocked
Understand CORS is a server rule, so the browser is doing its job, not breaking
Check the Network tab: the request may have succeeded but the browser hid the response
If you own the server, add the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header there
If you do not own it, route the request through your own backend (a proxy) instead
Re-test and confirm the response is now readable
tips: You cannot fix CORS from front-end JS alone; it must change on the server or via a proxy

triggers: setTimeout in loop prints same number
guides.title: setTimeout inside a loop logs the wrong number
steps: Confirm the symptom: all the timers print the final loop value
Check whether the loop uses var for the counter
Change var to let so each loop iteration gets its own copy of the variable
Re-run; each timer should now print its own number
If you must keep var, wrap the body in an IIFE that captures the current value
Confirm the printed values now increase as expected
tips: let is block-scoped per iteration; var is shared across the whole loop

guides.title: Node says it cannot find a module
steps: Read the error to see the exact module name it wants
If it is a package, run npm install <name> and check it appears in package.json
If it is your own file, check the relative path and that you included ./ at the start
Confirm the file extension and capitalization match exactly (case matters on Linux)
Make sure you are running node from the right folder
Re-run after fixing the path or installing the package
tips: ./file points to your own code; bare names like express look in node_modules

guides.title: Node server says the port is already in use
steps: Read the error; EADDRINUSE means something already listens on that port
Find the other process: on Mac/Linux run lsof -i :3000, on Windows run netstat -ano
Stop that process, or pick a different port number in your code
If it is a stuck old copy of your own server, kill it and restart
Consider reading the port from process.env.PORT so it is easy to change
Re-run and confirm the server starts cleanly
tips: A crashed previous run can hold the port; killing the old process usually frees it

guides.title: Cannot read properties of undefined
steps: Read the error to learn which property name failed (the part after 'reading')
Work backwards: the thing before the dot is undefined, find out why
console.log that object just before the failing line to see its real value
Check if it came from an array index that does not exist or a key that is misspelled
Use optional chaining obj?.prop or add an if-guard before reading it
Re-run and confirm the value exists before you use it
tips: The property in the message is the one you tried to read; the thing that is undefined is what comes before it

guides.title: Math gives NaN instead of a number
steps: Find the calculation that produces NaN and log every value going into it
Check if any input is undefined, a non-numeric string, or an empty input field
Remember input field values are strings; convert with Number() or parseFloat first
Confirm parseFloat of your string is not itself NaN before doing math
Add a fallback like Number(x) || 0 if a missing value should count as zero
Re-run and confirm you get a real number
tips: NaN is contagious: any math touching one NaN gives NaN, so find the first one

triggers: this not working in event handler
guides.title: this is undefined inside a callback or handler
steps: Log this inside the function to confirm what it points to
Remember a regular function gets its own this based on how it is called, not where it is written
Switch the callback to an arrow function, which keeps the surrounding this
If you cannot use an arrow function, bind it with .bind(this) when you pass it
For class methods, define them as arrow-function class fields to lock this
Re-run and confirm this now points to the object you expected
tips: Arrow functions do not have their own this; they borrow it from where they were written

triggers: array undefined at end of loop
guides.title: Loop misses an item or reads undefined at the end
steps: Check the loop condition: <= length reads one past the end, < length is correct
Remember arrays start at index 0, so the last valid index is length - 1
Log i and arr[i] each pass to see exactly where it goes wrong
If you skip the first item, you probably started at 1 instead of 0
Fix the start index or the comparison operator
Re-run and confirm every item is visited exactly once
tips: For an array of length 5, valid indexes are 0 through 4; index 5 is undefined

guides.title: Plus joins strings instead of adding numbers
steps: Confirm the symptom: 2 + 2 shows 22, not 4
Log typeof on each value; a string will show 'string'
Find where the value became a string, often an input field or JSON
Convert with Number() or parseFloat before adding
Be careful with + because it both adds numbers and joins strings
Re-run and confirm the addition is correct
tips: + joins if either side is a string; use Number() to force math

guides.title: Page does not update when you set innerHTML
steps: Confirm the element was actually found: log the result of getElementById/querySelector
If it is null, your script ran before the element existed, or the selector is wrong
Move the script to the bottom of the body or wrap it in DOMContentLoaded
Double-check the id or class name matches the HTML exactly
Confirm you set .innerHTML on the element, not on the variable holding the string
Re-run and confirm the page changes
tips: null means the element was not found; check the selector and when the script runs

guides.title: Unhandled promise rejection warning
steps: Read the warning to see which error was thrown but never caught
Find the async call or .then chain that can fail
Add a try/catch around your await calls, or a .catch on the Promise chain
Inside the catch, log the error so you can see what really happened
Make sure the catch is on the outermost call, not buried inside
Re-run and confirm the warning is gone and the error is handled
tips: Every Promise that can fail needs either a .catch or a surrounding try/catch with await

guides.title: A callback uses an old, stale value
steps: Log the variable inside the callback and compare it to the current value
Understand the function captured the value from when it was created, not now
If the value changes over time, read it fresh from a source instead of capturing it
Move the variable read INSIDE the callback so it grabs the latest value
For event handlers, store changing data on an object you read each time
Re-run and confirm the callback sees the current value
tips: A closure freezes the variables it can see at creation time unless you re-read them

triggers: cannot use import outside a module
guides.title: Mixing require and import causes errors
steps: Read the error: 'cannot use import' or 'require is not defined' tells you which style Node expected
Check package.json for "type": "module" (means use import) or its absence (means use require)
Pick one style and use it consistently in that file
If using ES modules (import), add file extensions like ./utils.js to your imports
If you must mix, name CommonJS files .cjs and module files .mjs
Re-run after making the styles consistent
tips: "type": "module" in package.json switches the whole project to import/export

triggers: cannot read saved object from localStorage
guides.title: localStorage stores [object Object] instead of your data
steps: Confirm the symptom: reading back gives the literal text [object Object]
Remember localStorage only stores strings, so objects get turned into that text
When saving, wrap the value in JSON.stringify(obj)
When reading, wrap the value in JSON.parse(stored)
Guard the parse: if the stored value is null, do not parse it
Re-run and confirm your object comes back correctly
tips: Save with JSON.stringify, read with JSON.parse; localStorage never stores real objects

guides.title: querySelector returns null for an element you can see
steps: Confirm the result is null by logging it
Check your selector syntax: querySelector needs . for classes and # for ids
getElementById takes the bare id with no # symbol; do not mix them up
Confirm the element exists in the HTML when the script runs (timing matters)
Check for typos and exact capitalization in the id or class
Re-run and confirm the element is found
tips: querySelector('.box') for class, querySelector('#box') for id, getElementById('box') for id without #

guides.title: Array.map produces undefined values
steps: Log the result of map to confirm it is an array of undefined
Check the callback function: did you forget the return statement?
If you used curly braces { }, you must write return explicitly
If you used a one-line arrow with no braces, the value returns automatically
Make sure you are not calling forEach when you meant map
Re-run and confirm map returns the transformed values
tips: x => x * 2 returns automatically; x => { x * 2 } returns undefined because it needs a return keyword

guides.title: Ignoring the error in a Node callback
steps: Look at the callback signature: Node uses (err, data) with the error first
Confirm you are actually checking err before using data
Add an if (err) block that logs or handles the error and then returns
Without the return, code keeps running with bad data after an error
Consider switching to the promise version with await and try/catch for cleaner code
Re-run and confirm errors are caught instead of crashing later
tips: The first callback argument is always the error in classic Node APIs; check it first

guides.title: Comparison with == gives a surprising result
steps: Log both values and their typeof to see if types differ
Remember == converts types before comparing, causing surprises like 0 == ''
Switch == to === and != to !== so types must match
Re-test the comparison with strict equality
If you really need a type conversion, do it explicitly with Number() or String() first
Confirm the comparison now behaves as expected
tips: Use === almost always; == can make '' == 0 and '0' == false both true

guides.title: Page reloads or navigates when you click a button or submit
steps: Confirm the page reloads or jumps when you interact
Check if it is a form submit or an anchor link triggering the default action
Add event parameter to your handler and call event.preventDefault() at the top
Make sure the handler is bound to the submit event for forms, not just the button
Confirm the default navigation no longer happens
Re-test by clicking and watching the URL stay the same
tips: Forms reload by default on submit; preventDefault() stops it so your JS can run

guides.title: process.env value is undefined
steps: Log process.env.MY_VAR to confirm it is undefined
If using a .env file, confirm you called require('dotenv').config() at the very top, before reading the variable
Check the .env file name is exactly .env and is in the project root
Confirm the variable name matches exactly, including capitalization
Make sure .env is not accidentally ignored by being missing on the server
Re-run with the variable loaded before it is used
tips: dotenv must run before you read any env var; put config() at the top of your entry file

guides.title: 0.1 + 0.2 does not equal 0.3
steps: Confirm the symptom: the result is 0.30000000000000004
Understand computers store decimals in binary and cannot represent all of them exactly
For display, round with (value).toFixed(2) to get a clean string
For comparisons, check if the difference is tiny: Math.abs(a - b) < 0.0001
For money, work in whole cents (integers) and divide by 100 only when showing
Re-run and confirm the value displays or compares correctly
tips: Never compare floats with === ; check that they are close enough instead

guides.title: Click handler runs immediately on page load
steps: Confirm the handler ran once at load even with no click
Look at how you passed it: addEventListener('click', myFunc()) with () calls it now
Remove the parentheses so you pass the function itself: addEventListener('click', myFunc)
If you need to pass arguments, wrap it in an arrow: () => myFunc(arg)
Re-load the page and confirm nothing fires until you click
Then click and confirm it fires correctly
tips: myFunc passes the function; myFunc() calls it immediately and passes the result

guides.title: A required module comes back empty due to circular imports
steps: Notice that a required module's exports are undefined or partly missing
Map out which file requires which; look for A requires B and B requires A
Move the shared code into a third file that both A and B require
Or move the require statement inside the function that uses it, so it runs later
Confirm the export is now fully defined when used
Re-run and check the values are present
tips: Circular requires can hand you a half-built module; breaking the cycle is the real fix

guides.title: Adding or toggling a CSS class has no effect
steps: Log the element to confirm it is not null
Use element.classList.add('name'), .remove('name'), or .toggle('name')
Pass the class name WITHOUT the leading dot (use 'active', not '.active')
Open DevTools and inspect the element to see if the class actually appears
Confirm a CSS rule for that class actually exists and is more specific than others
Re-test and confirm the styling changes
tips: classList methods take the bare class name; the dot is only for selectors

guides.title: A regex with the g flag gives alternating results
steps: Confirm the symptom: calling .test() repeatedly flips between true and false
Understand a regex with the g flag remembers lastIndex between calls
If you only need a yes/no check, remove the g flag
Or create a fresh regex each time instead of reusing one variable
Or reset regex.lastIndex = 0 before each test
Re-run and confirm consistent results
tips: Global regexes are stateful; reuse without reset causes the on-off-on pattern

guides.title: File reads fail depending on where you run the script
steps: Read the ENOENT error to see the exact path Node tried
Log process.cwd() to see the current working directory
Realize relative paths are based on where you ran node, not where the file lives
Build a reliable path with path.join(__dirname, 'data.json')
For ES modules use import.meta.url with fileURLToPath instead of __dirname
Re-run from a different folder to confirm it still works
tips: __dirname is the script's folder; cwd is wherever you launched node from

guides.title: Confusing null and undefined breaks a check
steps: Log the value to see whether it is null or undefined
Remember undefined means never set; null means intentionally empty
If you want to catch both, use == null which matches both (a rare good use of ==)
Or check value === undefined and value === null separately if you care which
For default values, use the ?? operator which only kicks in for null or undefined
Re-test the check covers the case you actually have
tips: value == null is true for both null and undefined; ?? gives a default for both

triggers: nested object still shared after copy
guides.title: Copying an object still changes the original
steps: Confirm changing the copy also changed the original
Understand spread {...obj} and Object.assign make a SHALLOW copy
Realize nested objects and arrays are still shared by reference
If you only changed a top-level value, the copy should be safe; recheck
For nested data, copy each level, or use structuredClone(obj) for a deep copy
Re-test and confirm the original is no longer affected
tips: structuredClone makes a true deep copy in modern browsers and Node

guides.title: Template string shows ${var} as literal text
steps: Confirm the output literally shows ${name} instead of the value
Check that you used backticks ` ` not single or double quotes
Template literals only interpolate inside backticks
Confirm the variable inside ${ } is spelled correctly and is in scope
Replace any quotes around the string with backticks
Re-run and confirm the variable value appears
tips: Only backtick strings do ${ } interpolation; ordinary quotes treat it as plain text

guides.title: fs.readFile gives undefined content
steps: Notice fs.readFile is asynchronous; it does not return the data
Move your code that uses the data INTO the callback or await the promise version
If you want a simple return value, use fs.readFileSync (fine for startup/scripts)
If you used the callback form, read data from the callback's second argument
Pass an encoding like 'utf8' so you get a string instead of a Buffer
Re-run and confirm the content is defined where you use it
tips: fs.readFile needs a callback; fs.readFileSync returns directly but blocks the program

guides.title: Canvas drawing does nothing because context is null
steps: Log the canvas element and the context to find which is null
If the canvas is null, the script ran before the element existed or the id is wrong
If getContext returns null, you passed the wrong type string; use '2d'
Set the canvas width and height as attributes, not just CSS, so the drawing area is correct
Draw a simple test rectangle to confirm the context works
Re-run and confirm shapes appear
tips: CSS width stretches the canvas; the width attribute sets the actual pixel grid you draw on

guides.title: Reading a data-* attribute returns undefined
steps: Confirm element.dataset.something is undefined
Remember HTML attribute data-user-id becomes dataset.userId in JS (camelCase)
Check the conversion: dashes are removed and the next letter capitalized
Or read it directly with element.getAttribute('data-user-id') using the exact name
Confirm the attribute actually exists on the element you selected
Re-run and confirm the value reads correctly
tips: data-user-id in HTML is dataset.userId in JS; the dashes turn into capital letters

guides.title: A required file keeps returning old data
steps: Confirm the file on disk changed but require still gives old values
Understand Node caches modules after the first require for speed
For config that changes at runtime, read it with fs.readFile instead of require
If you must re-require, delete it from require.cache by its resolved path first
Better: restart the process, or use a watcher in development
Re-run and confirm you get fresh data
tips: require caches the result; fresh reads need fs or clearing require.cache

guides.title: setTimeout with 0 still runs after other code
steps: Confirm the symptom: a 0ms timer logs AFTER later lines of code
Understand setTimeout always waits until the current code finishes (the event loop)
If you needed it sooner, you probably do not need setTimeout at all
Use it on purpose to let the browser render or to break a long task into chunks
If ordering matters, restructure with Promises or just call the code directly
Re-run and confirm you understand the order now
tips: setTimeout(fn, 0) means 'as soon as the current code is done', not 'right now'

guides.title: Reading an input field gives an empty string
steps: Log the input element to confirm it was found and is not null
Confirm you read element.value, not element.text or element.innerHTML
Check WHEN you read it: reading on page load gets the empty starting value
Read the value inside an event handler like 'input' or on button click instead
Trim the value to handle accidental spaces
Re-test by typing and reading on a click
tips: Form fields use .value; div text uses .textContent; read .value when the event fires, not at load

guides.title: Node process crashes on an unexpected error
steps: Read the stack trace printed when it crashed to find the file and line
Reproduce the crash and note the input that triggers it
Wrap the risky code in try/catch and handle the error gracefully
For async code, add .catch or await inside try/catch
Avoid swallowing errors silently; log them so you can fix the root cause
Re-run with the same input and confirm it no longer crashes
tips: An uncaught error stops the whole process; catch it where it happens, not just globally

guides.title: Using a variable as an object key does not work
steps: Confirm obj.key uses the literal word 'key' not your variable's value
To use a variable as the key when reading, use bracket notation: obj[myVar]
To set a dynamic key when building an object, use { [myVar]: value }
Log the key variable to confirm it holds the string you expect
Avoid quotes around the variable, which would turn it into a literal string
Re-run and confirm the right property is read or set
tips: Dot notation uses a fixed name; square brackets let a variable choose the key

guides.title: Sorting numbers gives the wrong order
steps: Confirm the symptom: [1, 2, 10] sorts as [1, 10, 2]
Understand sort() compares as strings by default, so '10' comes before '2'
Pass a compare function: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b) for ascending
Use (a, b) => b - a for descending order
Confirm all items are numbers, not strings of numbers
Re-run and confirm numeric order is correct
tips: sort() is alphabetical unless you give it (a, b) => a - b to compare numbers

triggers: await is only valid in async
guides.title: await is only valid inside async functions error
steps: Read the error: await was used outside an async function
Wrap the awaiting code inside an async function and then call it
Or, in an ES module (type module), top-level await is allowed; switch to a module
Inside the async function, use try/catch to handle failures
Make sure you actually call the async function you created
Re-run and confirm the await works
tips: Top-level await works only in ES modules; otherwise wrap it in an async function

guides.title: Event handler gets the wrong element from a click
steps: Log event.target and event.currentTarget to see the difference
event.target is the exact thing clicked (maybe a child icon)
event.currentTarget is the element the listener is attached to
If you delegated on a parent, use event.target.closest('.item') to find the real item
Pick the property that matches what you need
Re-test by clicking on child elements
tips: target is what you clicked; currentTarget is where the listener lives; closest() walks up to the wrapper

guides.title: Reading an image's size gives 0
steps: Confirm img.width or naturalWidth reads 0 right after setting src
Understand the image has not finished downloading yet
Wrap your size-reading code in img.onload = () => { ... }
Set the onload handler BEFORE setting the src
Use naturalWidth/naturalHeight for the true pixel size
Re-test and confirm the size reads correctly after load
tips: Set onload before src; the image dimensions are unknown until it finishes loading

guides.title: Express matches the wrong route or always 404s
steps: List your routes in the order they are defined
Remember Express checks routes top to bottom and uses the first match
Move specific routes ABOVE general or wildcard ones like app.get('*')
Confirm the HTTP method (get/post) and exact path match the request
Add a console.log inside the route to confirm it is reached
Re-test the request and confirm the right route handles it
tips: A catch-all route placed too early will swallow every request after it

guides.title: A button click does nothing at all
steps: Open the console and check for errors that stop the script early
Confirm the script actually ran: add a log at the top of the file
Confirm the element was found: log it and check it is not null
Confirm addEventListener used the right event name like 'click'
Check the element id/selector matches the HTML exactly
Re-test the click after fixing the wiring
tips: A single earlier error can stop all later JS; always check the console first

guides.title: parseInt returns an unexpected number
steps: Log the string you pass to parseInt
Pass a radix as the second argument: parseInt(str, 10) for base 10
Remember parseInt stops at the first non-digit, so '12px' becomes 12
If you need decimals, use parseFloat or Number instead
Confirm the input does not have hidden spaces or letters
Re-run and confirm the number is correct
tips: Always give parseInt a radix of 10 to avoid surprises with leading zeros

guides.title: Reading a request body gives nothing in plain Node
steps: Understand the body arrives in chunks over time, not all at once
Listen for 'data' events and append each chunk to a string or array
Listen for the 'end' event and process the full body there
Only parse JSON inside the 'end' handler, once all data arrived
Add an 'error' listener on the stream too
Re-test with a real POST and confirm the body is complete
tips: Without a framework, request bodies must be collected from data events and assembled on end

guides.title: Date shows the wrong month (off by one)
steps: Confirm the month is one less than expected
Remember JavaScript months are zero-based: January is 0, December is 11
When creating a date with new Date(year, month, day), subtract 1 from the month
When reading getMonth(), add 1 to display the human month
Days and years are NOT zero-based, only months
Re-run and confirm the month is correct
tips: Months are 0-11 in JS; January is 0, so add or subtract 1 where humans expect 1-12

guides.title: A CSS class will not turn off
steps: Inspect the element in DevTools to see which classes are actually present
Confirm you call classList.remove with the exact class name, no dot
Check whether something re-adds the class right after you remove it
Look for a CSS !important rule overriding your removal effect
Confirm you are operating on the same element you think you are
Re-test the toggle and watch the class list change
tips: Inspect the live element; a class that reappears is being re-added somewhere else

guides.title: An async error silently crashes or exits Node
steps: Reproduce the exit and watch for an UnhandledPromiseRejection message
Find the async function whose Promise can reject
Add try/catch around the await, or .catch to the chain
Log the error inside the handler to learn the cause
Fix the underlying problem the error points to
Re-run and confirm it no longer exits unexpectedly
tips: Modern Node exits on unhandled rejections; every awaited call that can fail needs handling

guides.title: Array.filter returns all items or none
steps: Log the array filter returns and compare lengths
Check the callback returns true to KEEP and false to drop
If it returns all, your condition is always true; if none, always false
Make sure you used filter (keeps matching) not map (transforms)
Test the condition on one item by hand to confirm it is right
Re-run and confirm only the wanted items remain
tips: filter keeps items where the callback returns true; double-check the condition's logic

guides.title: Clicking a child also triggers the parent's handler
steps: Confirm both the child and parent handlers run on one click
Understand events bubble up from child to parent by default
If you want only the child to react, call event.stopPropagation() in the child handler
Be careful: stopping propagation can break event delegation elsewhere
Consider whether delegation on the parent is actually the cleaner design
Re-test and confirm only the intended handler runs
tips: Events bubble up the tree; stopPropagation() stops the climb but use it sparingly

guides.title: File content shows as a Buffer or garbled bytes
steps: Notice the output looks like <Buffer 48 65 6c ...> or odd symbols
Understand fs returns raw bytes (a Buffer) unless told the encoding
Pass 'utf8' as the encoding option to readFile/readFileSync
Or call .toString('utf8') on the Buffer you received
Confirm the file is actually text and not a binary file
Re-run and confirm readable text
tips: Add 'utf8' so fs returns a string instead of a raw Buffer of bytes

guides.title: Identifier has already been declared error
steps: Read the error to find which name is declared twice
Search your files for two declarations of that name with let, const, or class
Two script tags sharing the global scope can collide on the same name
Rename one, or wrap each script's code in its own block or module
Switch to ES modules so each file has its own scope
Re-run and confirm the collision is gone
tips: Top-level let/const in two scripts share one global scope; modules isolate them

guides.title: Maximum call stack size exceeded
steps: Read the error: a function called itself too many times
Find the recursive function and check it has a base case that stops
Confirm each call moves CLOSER to the base case (smaller input)
Add a log of the argument to watch it shrink toward the stop point
If it never shrinks, fix the recursive step so it makes progress
Re-run and confirm it terminates
tips: Every recursion needs a base case AND progress toward it, or it never stops

guides.title: Cannot destructure property of undefined
steps: Read the error to see what you tried to destructure
The thing on the right of = was undefined or null
Log that value to learn why it is missing (bad fetch, wrong key, async timing)
Add a default: const { a } = obj || {} to avoid the crash
Better, fix why the object is undefined in the first place
Re-run and confirm the object exists before destructuring
tips: Destructuring null or undefined throws; provide a default like || {} or fix the source

guides.title: Command-line arguments come out wrong
steps: Log process.argv to see the full array
Note index 0 is the node binary and index 1 is your script path
Your real arguments start at index 2: process.argv.slice(2)
Remember every argument is a string; convert numbers with Number()
Handle missing arguments with a default value
Re-run and confirm you read the right values
tips: Real CLI args start at process.argv[2]; the first two slots are node and the script

guides.title: String includes/search misses matches due to case
steps: Confirm the symptom: 'Hello'.includes('hello') is false
Understand string search is case-sensitive by default
Lowercase both sides before comparing: str.toLowerCase().includes(term.toLowerCase())
Trim whitespace too if the input might have stray spaces
For partial word matching, confirm includes is what you want vs startsWith
Re-test with mixed-case input
tips: Normalize both strings with toLowerCase() before includes() to ignore case

guides.title: setInterval keeps running after you try to stop it
steps: Confirm the interval still fires after you expected it to stop
Save the id returned by setInterval into a variable
Call clearInterval(theId) with that exact saved id
Make sure you are not creating a new interval every time a function runs
Check you are not overwriting the id variable before clearing it
Re-test and confirm the timer stops
tips: You must keep the id returned by setInterval to clear it; clearing requires the right id

guides.title: Async results come back in a scrambled order
steps: Confirm the symptom: results print in a different order than the inputs
Understand parallel async calls finish whenever they finish, not in start order
If order matters, await them one at a time in a for...of loop
If you want speed AND order, use Promise.all which preserves input order in its result array
Map each input to a Promise, then await Promise.all on that array
Re-run and confirm the output array matches the input order
tips: Promise.all keeps results in the order of the input array even though they finish at different times

guides.title: removeEventListener does not remove the handler
steps: Confirm the handler still fires after you tried to remove it
Check if you passed an inline arrow or anonymous function to both add and remove
Each anonymous function is a different object, so remove cannot find a match
Store the handler in a named variable and pass that same variable to both add and remove
Confirm the event type and options match exactly between add and remove
Re-test and confirm it is removed
tips: removeEventListener needs the exact same function reference you added, not a look-alike

guides.title: HTML tags appear as literal text on the page
steps: Confirm the page shows hi as text, not as bold
Check whether you used textContent, which escapes HTML on purpose
If you truly want HTML rendered, use innerHTML instead
If the content came from a user, prefer textContent to stay safe
Confirm the string actually contains the tags you expect
Re-test and confirm the rendering you wanted
tips: textContent shows tags as text (safe); innerHTML renders them (use only with trusted content)

guides.title: A built file path has wrong or doubled slashes
steps: Log the final path string you built
Notice manual string concat with / can produce // or wrong slashes on Windows
Use path.join(a, b, c) which inserts the correct separator for the OS
Use path.resolve for an absolute path from the current directory
Avoid hardcoding / or backslash separators
Re-run and confirm the path is correct on your platform
tips: path.join handles separators for every OS; never glue path pieces with + and /

guides.title: find gives one item when you expected an array
steps: Confirm you got a single item (or undefined), not an array
Remember find returns the FIRST match or undefined
filter returns an ARRAY of all matches (possibly empty)
Pick find for one item, filter for many
If find returns undefined, no item matched; handle that case
Re-run with the correct method for your goal
tips: find = first match or undefined; filter = array of all matches

guides.title: Promise.all fails entirely when one Promise rejects
steps: Confirm the symptom: one failure throws and you lose all results
Understand Promise.all rejects as soon as any single Promise rejects
If you want all results including failures, use Promise.allSettled instead
allSettled returns an array of {status, value/reason} for each
Loop the results and handle fulfilled and rejected separately
Re-run and confirm you get partial results
tips: Promise.allSettled never short-circuits; it reports success and failure for every item

guides.title: Requiring a JSON file throws a syntax error
steps: Read the error; it usually names the position of the bad token
Open the JSON file and check for trailing commas, which JSON forbids
Confirm all keys and strings use double quotes, never single quotes
Remove any comments; JSON does not allow them
Run the file through a JSON validator to spot the exact issue
Re-run after fixing the JSON
tips: JSON is strict: double quotes, no trailing commas, no comments

guides.title: Modulo gives a negative result you did not expect
steps: Confirm the symptom: -1 % 5 gives -1, not 4
Understand JS % keeps the sign of the left operand
For a result that is always 0 or positive, use ((n % m) + m) % m
Use this when wrapping an index around an array, for example
Test with a few negative inputs to confirm
Re-run and confirm the wrapped value is correct
tips: For a positive wrap-around, use ((n % m) + m) % m instead of plain %

guides.title: Cannot access a variable before initialization
steps: Read the error naming the variable used too early
Find where it is declared with let or const
Realize let/const cannot be used in the lines ABOVE their declaration
Move the usage to after the declaration, or move the declaration up
Avoid relying on hoisting like you could with var
Re-run and confirm the order is fixed
tips: let and const exist but cannot be touched before their declaration line (the temporal dead zone)

guides.title: Not sure if the server actually started
steps: Add a callback to listen: app.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on 3000'))
Run the program and confirm you see the log
If the log never appears, an earlier error stopped the code; check the console
Visit the URL in a browser to confirm a response
Check the Network tab or use curl to test the endpoint
Confirm the port matches what you typed in the browser
tips: A listen callback gives you a clear 'I am up' signal so you stop guessing

triggers: pushing to array does not re-render
guides.title: UI does not update after changing an array in place
steps: Confirm the data changed but the screen did not
Many UI patterns only notice a NEW array, not an in-place push/splice
Create a new array instead: const next = [...old, item]
Assign the new array back to the state or variable the UI reads
Avoid push/splice on the tracked array; build a fresh copy
Re-test and confirm the UI updates
tips: Replace the array with a copy ([...old, item]) so change-detection sees a new reference

guides.title: Script runs before the page elements exist
steps: Confirm elements are null when the script first runs
Move your <script> tag to the bottom of the body, after the elements
Or wrap your code in document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', ...)
Use DOMContentLoaded (fires when HTML is parsed) rather than window.load (waits for images too)
Confirm the elements are found inside that handler
Re-test and confirm the script works
tips: DOMContentLoaded fires when the HTML is ready; window.load waits for every image and asset

guides.title: An async function never seems to run
steps: Confirm you actually CALLED the function with parentheses, not just defined it
Defining async function main() does nothing until you call main()
Add main() (or main().catch(console.error)) after the definition
Add a log on the first line to confirm it entered
Make sure no earlier error stopped execution
Re-run and confirm it runs
tips: Defining a function is not running it; an async function still needs to be called

guides.title: x.method is not a function error
steps: Read the error: the thing you called is not a function
Log the object and the property to see its real type
Maybe the property is undefined, a string, or you misspelled the method name
Confirm the object is the type you think (array vs object vs string)
Guard with optional chaining for calls: obj.method?.() if it might be missing
Re-run and confirm the method exists before calling
tips: 'is not a function' means that property exists but is not callable; check its type and spelling

triggers: map is not a function nodelist
guides.title: Looping over querySelectorAll results fails
steps: Confirm the error mentions map or another array method on the result
querySelectorAll returns a NodeList, which supports forEach but NOT map/filter directly
Use forEach to loop, or convert with Array.from(nodeList) first
After Array.from you can use map, filter, and the rest
Confirm the selector actually matched elements (length > 0)
Re-run and confirm the loop works
tips: A NodeList has forEach but not map; wrap it in Array.from() for full array methods

guides.title: An HTTP request hangs forever
steps: Confirm the browser keeps spinning and never gets a response
Check that every code path calls res.end() or res.send() exactly once
An if-branch that forgets to respond leaves the request open
Add a log right before the response to confirm that path is reached
Make sure you do not call the response twice, which also causes errors
Re-run and confirm the request completes
tips: Every request must send exactly one response; a missed res.end leaves it hanging

guides.title: includes never finds an object in an array
steps: Confirm includes returns false even though a matching object is there
Understand includes compares objects by reference, not by their contents
Two objects with the same fields are still different references
Use arr.some(item => item.id === target.id) to compare by a field
Or find the item with arr.find using the same field comparison
Re-test and confirm the match is found
tips: includes matches primitives by value but objects only by exact reference; compare a key field instead

guides.title: State leaks between requests on a Node server
steps: Confirm one user's data shows up for another, or values persist oddly
Look for variables declared at module top level that you reassign per request
Module-level variables are SHARED across all requests
Move per-request data inside the request handler so each call gets its own
Use the request/response objects to carry per-request state
Re-test with two requests and confirm no bleed-over
tips: Top-level variables are shared by every request; put per-request data inside the handler

guides.title: preventDefault does nothing on a scroll/touch event
steps: Check the console for a warning about a passive event listener
Modern browsers make scroll/touch listeners passive by default for speed
A passive listener ignores preventDefault
Pass { passive: false } as the third argument to addEventListener
Only do this when you truly need to block scrolling, since it can hurt performance
Re-test and confirm preventDefault now works
tips: Touch/scroll listeners are passive by default; add { passive: false } to allow preventDefault

guides.title: String replace only changes the first match
steps: Confirm only the first occurrence changed
Understand replace with a plain string only changes the first match
Use replaceAll(old, new) to change every occurrence
Or use a regex with the g flag: replace(/old/g, 'new')
Watch for special regex characters if you switch to a regex
Re-run and confirm all matches changed
tips: replace changes one; replaceAll (or a /g regex) changes them all

guides.title: Too many open files or handles error
steps: Read the error like EMFILE 'too many open files'
Find resources you open in a loop: files, database connections, sockets
Confirm you close or release each one when done (close the file, return the connection)
Prefer try/finally so resources close even when an error happens
Avoid opening new connections per request; reuse a pool
Re-run and confirm handles stay under control
tips: Use try/finally to guarantee files and connections close even on error

guides.title: Reading a checkbox gives 'on' instead of checked state
steps: Confirm element.value returns 'on' regardless of checked state
For checkboxes, read element.checked (true/false), not element.value
For radio groups, find the one that is checked, then read its value
Use querySelector('input[name=group]:checked') to get the selected radio
Confirm the input name groups the radios together
Re-test by toggling and reading checked
tips: Checkboxes use .checked for state; .value is just the form value when checked

triggers: need await at top of file
guides.title: Need to await something at the top of a script
steps: Confirm you cannot use await directly because you are not in an async function or module
Wrap the code in an immediately-invoked async function: (async () => { ... })()
Put your awaits inside that wrapper
Add .catch or a try/catch so errors are not silently lost
Or convert the file to an ES module and use top-level await
Re-run and confirm the awaited code runs
tips: (async () => { await thing(); })() lets you await in a place that is not already async

guides.title: JSON.stringify throws on a circular structure
steps: Read the error: 'Converting circular structure to JSON'
Find the object that references itself, directly or through a chain
Decide which fields you actually need to serialize
Build a plain object with just those fields and stringify that
Or pass a replacer function to JSON.stringify to skip the circular parts
